correspondence.no-real-lorentzian-vacuum.formal: Let $(\hb, \Omega)$ be a gravitational field on flat spacetime (Definition \claimref{obj.synthesis.gtg-flat-spacetime-gauge-fields}), $\mathcal{W}$ the Weyl map of its field strength on physical bivectors, and $\Lambda^{\pm}$ the duality halves, the eigenspaces of multiplication by the pseudoscalar $I$ (the Hodge star) on the bivectors complexified by the central pseudoscalar $I_5$ of $\Cl(2,3)$, $\Lambda^{2}_{\C} = \Lambda^{2} \oplus \Lambda^{2}I_5$ ($I_5$ commutes with every spacetime vector and is kept distinct from $I$; complex conjugation is $I_5 \mapsto -I_5$). At every point of the invertible region, if either duality half of $\mathcal{W}$ vanishes, $\mathcal{W}$ vanishes: a real half-flat field has a conformally flat derived metric. The statement is pointwise; equivalently, on an oriented Lorentzian $4$-manifold, if either duality half of the Weyl tensor vanishes, the Weyl tensor vanishes: a real Lorentzian half-flat metric is conformally flat. (This is classical, and is the reason the nonlinear graviton is stated for complex or Riemannian signature in \cite{Penrose76}; the proof is included because it is four lines.) In particular no real Lorentzian black hole is half-flat: the Weyl maps of the Schwarzschild and Kerr fields are nonzero (a nonzero curvature scale times a nonzero type-D bivector off the singular locus, the locus where $\hb$ fails, imported from \cite[Prop.~3.3, Fact 6.3]{ButlerT6}).
correspondence.no-real-lorentzian-vacuum.technical:
For a gravitational field on flat spacetime, duality on bivectors is multiplication by the pseudoscalar $I$, the Hodge star of the derived metric, a complex structure on bivectors; on the bivectors complexified by the central pseudoscalar $I_5$ of $\Cl(2,3)$, distinct from $I$, its eigenspaces $\Lambda^\pm$ are interchanged by complex conjugation. The real Weyl map $\mathcal{W}$ of the field strength commutes with $I$, so it preserves $\Lambda^\pm$, and its restrictions $\mathcal{W}^\pm$ are complex conjugates of each other. Hence $\mathcal{W}^- = 0$ forces $\mathcal{W}^+ = 0$ and so $\mathcal{W} = 0$, and by Weyl's theorem the derived metric of a real half-flat field is conformally flat. In manifold language: on an oriented Lorentzian four-manifold a real half-flat metric is conformally flat.

In particular no real Lorentzian black hole is half-flat: the Weyl maps of the Schwarzschild and Kerr fields are a nonzero curvature scale times a nonzero type-D bivector off the singular locus. The result is classical, and is the reason the nonlinear graviton is stated for complex or Riemannian signature.
correspondence.no-real-lorentzian-vacuum.lay: In four dimensions the part of the gravitational field strength that describes tidal forces splits into two mirror-image halves. For a real gravitational field with one time direction the two halves are complex conjugates, so if one vanishes so does the other, and the geometry the field describes is then flat up to a change of scale. Real black holes such as Schwarzschild and Kerr are therefore never half-flat, which is why Penrose's construction of such spaces from spinor geometry (the nonlinear graviton) is stated only in complex or Euclidean settings.

proofs.main:
Containment is immediate: $B_i \in \Lambda^2 W$ and $\Lambda^2 W$ is a subalgebra (brackets of operators preserving $W$ and annihilating $W^\perp$ do the same). For fullness, compute with $(u \wedge v)(w) \;=\; \ip{v}{w}\,u - \ip{u}{w}\,v$, the action of bivectors on vectors as the orthogonal Lie algebra (\claimref{std-algebra.bivector-lie-algebra}): for $u, v, w$ orthogonal frame vectors,
\[
[\,u\wedge v,\ v\wedge w\,] \;=\; Q(v)\; u\wedge w ,
\]
and brackets of wedges with no shared factor vanish. Hence $[B_1, B_2] = [e_0\wedge e_1,\, e_0 \wedge e_2]$: rewriting $B_1 = -e_1\wedge e_0$, this is $-Q(e_0)\, e_1\wedge e_2 = -R_{12}$, and cyclically for the other pairs: all three rotations appear. Then $[R_{12}, B_2] = [e_1\wedge e_2, e_0\wedge e_2]$ $= -[e_1\wedge e_2,\, e_2\wedge e_0] = -Q(e_2)\,e_1\wedge e_0 = -B_1$ recovers the boosts, and the six elements $\{B_i, R_{ij}\}$ are a basis of $\Lambda^2 W$. The verification script performs the generation exactly: starting from the three boosts as antisymmetric matrices over $\mathbb{Q}$ preserving the $(2,4)$ form, it closes under commutators and confirms the resulting span has dimension six and lies in $\Lambda^2 W$.

The existence of some parallel null tractor is strictly weaker: it says only that $[g]$ is almost Ricci-flat, and a non-constant rescaling $e^{2\omega}g$ keeps a parallel section while losing the field equations. interior.covariant-form-vacuum-equations.lay: In the interior region, Einstein's equations for empty space can be recast as a single condition on the gravitational fields: a particular marker in the six-dimensional conformal extension of spacetime, attached to the physical scale, must stay constant as it is carried from point to point by a gauge field built from gravity. This result proves that the two formulations are exactly equivalent, and that the marker is a null (lightlike) object. It also notes that merely having some constant marker of this kind is a weaker condition that does not by itself give the field equations.

interior.exact-scale-decoupling.formal:
In the conventions of Fact \claimref{interior.imported-schwarzschild-curvature-spectrum}, the Schwarzschild curvature operator is, exactly and at every radius,
\[
\mathcal{R}(B) \;=\; -\,\frac{M}{r^3}\,S(B), \qquad
S \;:=\; 1 - 3\Pi \;=\; -\tfrac12\bigl(B \mapsto B + 3\,\sigma_r B \sigma_r\bigr),
\]
where the shape operator $S$ satisfies the algebraic identity
\[
S^2 + S = 2 ,
\]
has spectrum $(-2, -2, 1, 1, 1, 1)$, and is trace-free. The factorisation is exact: $S$ depends on neither $M$ nor $r$, and the entire approach to the singularity changes only the conformal prefactor $-M/r^3$.
interior.exact-scale-decoupling.technical:
Let $\Pi$ project the six-dimensional bivector space onto the pair $\operatorname{span}\{\sigma_r, I\sigma_r\}$ formed by the radial boost plane and its dual. Given the imported Schwarzschild spectrum, the curvature operator factorises exactly, at every radius, as $\mathcal{R}(B) = -\frac{M}{r^3}\,S(B)$ with $S = 1 - 3\Pi = -\tfrac12(B \mapsto B + 3\,\sigma_r B\sigma_r)$.

The shape operator obeys $S^2 + S = 2$, has spectrum $(-2,-2,1,1,1,1)$ and is trace-free. It depends on neither $M$ nor $r$, so the whole approach to the singularity changes only the conformal prefactor $-M/r^3$. The singularity paper proves the same identity in its Theorem on the curvature of the gauge field (\claimref{singularity.curvature-gauge-field-exact-shape-decoupling}), adding that the doubled eigenvalue sits exactly on the radial boost plane and its dual.
interior.exact-scale-decoupling.lay: Near a Schwarzschild black hole the tidal curvature has a fixed pattern: stretching in one pair of directions and squeezing in the others, in a two-to-one ratio. This result shows the pattern is exactly the same at every radius, all the way in towards the singularity. Only its overall strength, which grows like the inverse cube of the radius, changes.
interior.exact-scale-decoupling.typing_note: The single use, the imported curvature spectrum, is a genuine premise; the paper notes the classic 2:1 tidal structure but does not say the operator identity itself is obtained classically, so no standard-route was added.

proofs.main: First the algebra of conjugation by $\sigma_r$. For $B$ in the plane pair: $\sigma_r\,\sigma_r\,\sigma_r = \sigma_r$ since $\sigma_r^2 = 1$; and $\sigma_r (I\sigma_r)\sigma_r = I\,\sigma_r^3 = I\sigma_r$ since $I$ commutes with even elements. For each of the four mixed planes, $B$ anticommutes with $\sigma_r$: writing $B = \gamma_a\gamma_b$ with exactly one index in $\{0,1\}$, the product $\sigma_r B$ reorders by two transpositions against one shared and one distinct generator, producing a net sign $-1$, so $\sigma_r B = -B\sigma_r$ and $\sigma_r B \sigma_r = -B\sigma_r^2 = -B$. Hence $-\tfrac12(B + 3\sigma_r B\sigma_r)$ equals $-2B$ on the plane pair and $+B$ on the mixed planes, which is $1 - 3\Pi$. Fact \claimref{interior.imported-schwarzschild-curvature-spectrum} says the curvature is diagonal on exactly these planes with eigenvalues $2M/r^3$ (doubled magnitude, on the pair) and $-M/r^3$ (mixed); since $1 - 3\Pi$ has eigenvalues $-2$ on the pair and $+1$ on the mixed planes, the operator with those eigenvalues is exactly $-\tfrac{M}{r^3}(1 - 3\Pi)$: so $\mathcal{R} = -(M/r^3)S$ in the conventions of Fact \claimref{interior.imported-schwarzschild-curvature-spectrum}, the store's curvature sign; only the eigenvalue ratio $2 : (-1)$ and the identity of the distinguished plane pair enter any later argument, and both are convention-free. The identity: $S^2 = (1 - 3\Pi)^2 = 1 - 6\Pi + 9\Pi^2 = 1 + 3\Pi$ since $\Pi^2 = \Pi$, so $S^2 + S = 2$. Spectrum and trace: eigenvalue $1 - 3 = -2$ on the two-dimensional range of $\Pi$ and $+1$ on its four-dimensional kernel; trace $= 4 - 4 = 0$.

interior.imported-equivalence-einstein-e.formal: On any region where $\hb$ is invertible, the GTG field equations for $(\hb, \Omega)$ are equivalent to the Einstein field equations for the metric $g(a,b) = \hb^{-1}(a)\cdot\hb^{-1}(b)$; in vacuum, to Ricci-flatness of $g$. \emph{Provenance:} Lasenby, Doran and Gull \cite[\S 4.3 and App.~C]{LDG1998}; textbook form \cite[Ch.~13-14]{DoranLasenby2003}.
interior.imported-equivalence-einstein-e.technical: On any region where the gauge field $\hb$ is invertible, the field equations of gauge theory gravity (GTG) for $(\hb, \Omega)$ are equivalent to the Einstein field equations for the metric $g(a,b) = \hb^{-1}(a)\cdot\hb^{-1}(b)$. In vacuum they are equivalent to Ricci-flatness of $g$. This is imported from the gauge-theory-gravity literature.
interior.imported-equivalence-einstein-e.lay: Gauge theory gravity rewrites general relativity in the language of geometric algebra. This imported result says that, wherever its basic field can be inverted, its equations say exactly the same as Einstein's equations for the corresponding metric. In empty space this means the metric has vanishing Ricci curvature.

interior.imported-schwarzschild-curvatur.formal: For the Schwarzschild gravitational field $(\hb, \Omega)$ on flat spacetime in the static gauge, whose derived metric is the static spherically symmetric vacuum metric $f\,dt_s^2 - f^{-1}dr^2 - r^2(d\theta^2 + \sin^2\theta\,d\varphi^2)$ with $f = 1 - 2M/r$ (Definition \claimref{obj.synthesis.gtg-flat-spacetime-gauge-fields}), the curvature operator $B \mapsto \mathcal{R}(B)$ on physical bivectors, in the store's sign, is diagonal on the coordinate planes of the static orthonormal frame of physical vectors, with eigenvalue of one magnitude, $2M/r^3$, on the radial boost plane $\sigma_r$ and its Hodge dual $I\sigma_r$, and eigenvalue of half that magnitude and opposite sign, $-M/r^3$, on the four mixed planes. \emph{Provenance:} the radial-plane eigenvalue from the gauge field alone in \cite[Prop.~2.4(1)]{ButlerT5}; the mixed- and angular-plane eigenvalues by the Cartan structure equations in the static chart in \cite[App.~A]{ButlerT5}, the two computations agreeing on the invertible region by Fact \claimref{interior.imported-equivalence-einstein-equations}; the same computation in the GTG literature is \cite[Ch.~14]{DoranLasenby2003}.
interior.imported-schwarzschild-curvatur.technical:
For the Schwarzschild field on flat spacetime in the static gauge, with derived metric $f\,dt_s^2 - f^{-1}dr^2 - r^2(d\theta^2 + \sin^2\theta\,d\varphi^2)$ and $f = 1 - 2M/r$, the field strength read as the curvature operator $\mathcal{R}(B)$ on physical bivectors is diagonal on the coordinate planes of the static orthonormal frame. Its eigenvalue is $2M/r^3$ on the radial boost plane $\sigma_r$ and its dual $I\sigma_r$, and $-M/r^3$ on the four mixed planes.

The radial-plane value comes from the gauge field alone, the others from the Cartan structure equations in the static chart, and the two computations agree on the invertible region by the equivalence of the gauge field equations with Einstein's. The same computation appears in the gauge theory gravity literature.
interior.imported-schwarzschild-curvatur.lay: The tidal part of the gravitational field strength around a non-rotating black hole has a simple form: one pair of planes feels a stretching or squeezing of one strength, and the four remaining mixed planes feel half that strength with the opposite sign. This standard result is restated from earlier work in the series.

interior.imported-tractor-connection.lay: Gravity here is a pair of fields on flat spacetime, and what it determines, once lengths are allowed to be rescaled freely, is a conformal geometry. interior.metric-parallelism-trace-schout.formal: Let $g$ be the derived metric of a gravitational field $(\hb, \Omega)$ on flat spacetime (Definition \claimref{obj.synthesis.gtg-flat-spacetime-gauge-fields}). (i) The connection \claimref{interior.imported-tractor-connection}, which on flat spacetime is the $\Cl(2,4)$ gauge field of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.gtg-tractor-gauge-field-reproduces-tractor-connection}, preserves the tractor metric $\ip{(\sigma,\mu,\rho)}{(\sigma,\mu,\rho)} \;=\; g(\mu,\mu) \,+\, 2\sigma\rho$, the square $Q$ of $\Cl(2,4)$. (ii) If $\Sch_{ab} = c\, g_{ab}$ for a function $c$, that is $\Sch(A) = c\,A$ for the Schouten map of the field strength, then $c = \tfrac{R}{24}$ and $\Ric_{ab} = \tfrac{R}{4} g_{ab}$, that is $\mathcal{R}(A) = \tfrac14\mathcal{R}\,A$; in particular $\Sch_{ab} = 0$ if and only if $\Ric_{ab} = 0$.
interior.metric-parallelism-trace-schout.technical:
(i) The tractor connection preserves the tractor metric. On flat spacetime the connection is a $\Cl(2,4)$ bivector-valued gauge field acting by the commutator product, an infinitesimal rotation, so it preserves $Q$; in index form, differentiating $Q(T)$ along any direction and substituting the connection, the genuine derivative terms reassemble the derivative of $Q(T)$, and the remaining terms cancel in pairs; the two Schouten terms are one contraction written with the index raised on either side, so no symmetry of $\Sch$ is needed.

(ii) For a gravitational field with derived metric $g$, if $\Sch_{ab} = c\,g_{ab}$ for a function $c$, tracing gives $c = R/24$, and substituting back gives $\Ric_{ab} = \tfrac{R}{4}g_{ab}$. In particular $\Sch_{ab} = 0$ if and only if $\Ric_{ab} = 0$.
interior.metric-parallelism-trace-schout.lay: This lemma records two elementary facts behind the tractor form of the gravitational field equations. First, the natural derivative on the tractor bundle, which on flat spacetime is a field of rotations of the six-dimensional conformal model, respects that model's own notion of length. Second, if the Schouten tensor, a rearranged form of the gravitational field strength, is a multiple of the metric then the field is Einstein, and the Schouten tensor vanishes exactly when the Ricci curvature does.
interior.metric-parallelism-trace-schout.typing_note: Added the tractor-connection fact: the lemma is about its displayed connection and Schouten formula (cited by equation reference, not claimref), and the proof computes with both.

proofs.main:
Read in Gauge Theory Gravity: the metric $g$ below is the derived metric of the gravitational field $(\hb, \Omega)$ on flat spacetime, the manifold is the invertible region, and the tractor connection is the flat-space $\Cl(2,4)$ gauge field of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.gtg-tractor-gauge-field-reproduces-tractor-connection}; the index computation below is its reading in the splitting of $g$ (Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-gtg-dictionary}).

(i) Along any direction $a$, with primes denoting the slots of \claimref{interior.imported-tractor-connection},
\[
\tfrac12\,\partial_a Q(T) \;=\; \sigma'\rho + \rho'\sigma + \mu^b\mu'_b
= (\nabla_a\sigma - \mu_a)\rho + (\nabla_a\rho + \Sch_a{}^b\mu_b)\sigma + \mu^b(\nabla_a\mu_b + g_{ab}\rho - \Sch_{ab}\sigma).
\]
The genuine derivative terms assemble to $\tfrac12\partial_a(2\sigma\rho + |\mu|^2)$; the remainder is $-\mu_a\rho + \mu_a \rho + \Sch_a{}^b\mu_b\sigma - \Sch_{ab}\mu^b\sigma = 0$, the two Schouten terms being one contraction written with the index raised on either side, so that no symmetry of $\Sch$ is needed.
(ii) Tracing $\Sch_{ab} = c\,g_{ab}$ gives $4c = \tfrac12(R - \tfrac{4R}{6}) = \tfrac{R}{6}$, so $c = \tfrac{R}{24}$; substituting back, $\Ric_{ab} = \tfrac{R}{6}g_{ab} + 2c\,g_{ab} = \tfrac{R}{4}g_{ab}$. If $c = 0$ then $R = 24c = 0$ and hence $\Ric = 0$; the converse is immediate.

interior.non-null-stabilisers-section-th.technical:
Let $I \in V$ with $Q(I) \neq 0$, so $V = \R I \oplus I^\perp$. Writing a bivector as $B = I\wedge u + C$ with $u \in I^\perp$ and $C \in \Lambda^2(I^\perp)$ gives $B(I) = -Q(I)\,u$, so the stabiliser is $\Lambda^2(I^\perp) \cong \mathfrak{so}(I^\perp)$: ten-dimensional and reductive, $\mathfrak{so}(1,4)$ for $Q(I) > 0$ and $\mathfrak{so}(2,3)$ for $Q(I) < 0$.

The section $M_I = \{X : Q(X) = 0,\ \ip{X}{I} = 1\}$ becomes, under $Y = X - I/Q(I)$, the pseudosphere $Q(Y) = -1/Q(I)$ in $I^\perp$: de Sitter space for $Q(I) > 0$ and anti-de Sitter space for $Q(I) < 0$, with the stabiliser acting as its isometry group. The polar hypersurface $\ip{X}{I} = 0$ meets the quadric in the projectivised null cone of $I^\perp$, a spacelike conformal infinity $S^3$ in the first case and a timelike one in the second.
interior.non-null-stabilisers-section-th.lay: In the series' six-dimensional ambient space, pick a direction whose squared length is not zero. The symmetries that leave it fixed are those of de Sitter space if the squared length is positive, or of anti-de Sitter space if it is negative. A natural slice of the space of points is then exactly that de Sitter or anti-de Sitter spacetime, and its boundary at infinity is spacelike or timelike accordingly.
interior.non-null-stabilisers-section-th.typing_note: Self-contained flat-model computation; no edges needed. Levels pass: conditions already kept.

proofs.main: (1) Write $B = I \wedge u + C$ with $u \in I^\perp$ and $C \in \Lambda^2(I^\perp)$, which is possible and unique since $Q(I) \neq 0$ splits $V = \R I \oplus I^\perp$. Then, with bivectors acting on vectors as in \claimref{std-algebra.bivector-lie-algebra}, $B(I) = \ip{u}{I}I - Q(I)u + 0 = -Q(I)\,u$, which vanishes iff $u = 0$. So the stabiliser is $\Lambda^2(I^\perp)$, and $I^\perp$ carries the restricted form: by \claimref{std-algebra.sylvester-inertia}, signature $(1,4)$ if $I$ is a plus direction, $(2,3)$ if a minus direction. Triviality of the nilradical is the reductivity of orthogonal algebras of nondegenerate forms. (2) For $X \in M_I$: $\ip{Y}{I} = \ip{X}{I} - 1 = 0$ and $Q(Y) = Q(X) - 2\ip{X}{I}/Q(I) + 1/Q(I) = -1/Q(I)$. The map is an affine bijection commuting with the stabiliser. If $Q(I) > 0$: $I^\perp \cong \R^{1,4}$ and the locus $Q(Y) = -1/Q(I) < 0$ is the standard de Sitter hyperboloid, with induced signature $(1,3)$ and isometry group $O(1,4)$. If $Q(I) < 0$: $I^\perp \cong \R^{2,3}$ and the locus $Q(Y) > 0$ is the standard anti-de Sitter hyperboloid with isometry group $O(2,3)$. (3) Null rays of $I^\perp$: for $\R^{1,4}$ with form $t^2 - \sum_1^4 x_i^2$, the null cone is $t^2 = |x|^2$, whose rays are parametrised by the unit sphere $S^3 = \{|x| = 1, t = 1\}$; the induced degenerate form on the cone descends to a negative-definite form on the ray space, i.e.\ a spacelike (Riemannian) conformal $3$-sphere, the conformal infinity of de Sitter space. For $\R^{2,3}$ the same construction yields ray space $S^1 \times S^2$ (up to cover) carrying a Lorentzian conformal structure: the timelike infinity of anti-de Sitter space.

interior.stabiliser-rotates-parabolic-re.technical:
The squared norm $Q(I_g) = \Lambda/3$ of the frozen point decides which orbit it lies on, and the flat-model stabiliser computations then identify its stabiliser in the structure group. For $\Lambda = 0$ it is the Poincar\'e group $SO(1,3) \ltimes \R^4$, with four-dimensional nilradical: the parabolic case, whose transvections are the obstruction structure of the series' element-level no-go theorem.

For $\Lambda > 0$ it is the de Sitter group $SO(1,4)$, reductive, acting on the Einstein section as its isometry group, with spacelike polar infinity the $3$-sphere $\ip{X}{I} = 0$; for $\Lambda < 0$ it is the anti-de Sitter group $SO(2,3)$, reductive, with timelike polar infinity. So $\Lambda$ measures precisely the failure of infinity to be parabolic.
interior.stabiliser-rotates-parabolic-re.lay: The symmetries that keep the frozen point fixed change character with the cosmological constant. With no cosmological constant they are the symmetries of flat spacetime, translations included; with a positive or negative one they become the symmetries of de Sitter or anti-de Sitter space, with no translations. The cosmological constant thus measures how far infinity is from the flat-space kind.
interior.stabiliser-rotates-parabolic-re.typing_note: All three uses are the results the proof combines; the no-go theorem is cited only to name the transvections, so it was not added.

The ambient bundle carries the canonical connection, whose expression in the scale $g$ is
\begin{equation}
\nabla_{a}(\sigma, \mu_{b}, \rho) = \bigl(\nabla_{a}\sigma - \mu_{a},\;\; \nabla_{a}\mu_{b} + g_{ab}\,\rho - P_{ab}\,\sigma,\;\; \nabla_{a}\rho + P_{a}{}^{b}\mu_{b}\bigr),
\end{equation}
and it preserves $\ip{(\sigma,\mu,\rho)}{(\sigma',\mu',\rho')} = \sigma\rho' + \rho\sigma' + g(\mu,\mu')$. On a vacuum Einstein background with cosmological constant $\Lambda$, in these conventions $P_{ab} = (\Lambda/6)\,g_{ab}$ and $J = 2\Lambda/3$, the bundle carries a distinguished parallel section $I$, the frozen point: in its own scale $I = (1, 0, \rho_{I})$ with vanishing middle slot, $\nabla I = 0$ is equivalent to the vacuum equations, and
\[
\rho_{I} = \frac{J}{n} = \frac{\Lambda}{6}, \qquad Q(I) = \frac{2J}{n} = \frac{\Lambda}{3}.
\]
(The geometry paper is four-dimensional; the general-$n$ form of $\rho_{I}$ is the middle slot of \claimref{mass.imported-frozen-point-tractor-connection} for the section $(1, 0, \rho_{I})$, $g_{ab}\rho_{I} = P_{ab}$, traced.) $I$ is null exactly when $\Lambda = 0$; for $\Lambda > 0$ its stabiliser is $SO(1,4)$ and the induced form on $I^{\perp}$ has signature $(1,4)$. \emph{Provenance:} \cite[Fact~4.1, Prop.~4.4, Thm.~4.5, Thm.~4.7, Prop.~4.10]{ButlerT6} (\claimref{interior.scale-tractor-leaves-cone}, \claimref{interior.stabiliser-rotates-parabolic-reductive}, \claimref{interior.non-null-stabilisers-section-they-act}, \claimref{interior.imported-tractor-connection}, \claimref{interior.covariant-form-vacuum-equations}) (Prop.~4.4 for the stabiliser algebra and the signature of $I^{\perp}$, Prop.~4.10 for the group). The sign of the norm is the series' convention, fixed there and machine-verified; \cite[Rem.~4.9]{ButlerT6} records why that sign is not free: a norm of the opposite sign could not carry the de Sitter stabiliser the same paper establishes. The relative sign of the Schouten slots in \claimref{mass.imported-frozen-point-tractor-connection} against the literature is convention-dependent and is fixed internally in the geometry paper \cite[Lem.~4.8]{ButlerT6} (\claimref{interior.sign-fixed-internally}); every formula of this paper is written in the convention of \claimref{mass.imported-frozen-point-tractor-connection}.

mass.imported-thomas-operator.formal:
Let $g$ be the derived metric of a gravitational field $(\hb, \Omega)$ on flat spacetime (Definition \claimref{obj.synthesis.gtg-flat-spacetime-gauge-fields}), with tractors the vectors $\sigma\nInf + \mu + \rho\nO$ of $\Cl(2,4)$. On a density $\sigma$ of conformal weight $w$ the Thomas operator $D$ produces the tractor
\[
D\sigma = \bigl(\, w(n+2w-2)\,\sigma,\;\; (n+2w-2)\,\nabla_{a}\sigma,\;\; -(\Box\sigma - wJ\sigma)\,\bigr)
\]
in the splitting of a scale $g$, and $D\sigma$ is conformally invariant as a weight-$(w-1)$ tractor field. For $w = 1$ and a scale $\sigma$, $\tfrac1n D\sigma$ is the scale tractor of $\sigma$, whose parallelism, for the tractor gauge field of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.gtg-tractor-gauge-field-reproduces-tractor-connection}, is the Einstein condition of Fact \claimref{mass.imported-frozen-point-tractor-connection}. \emph{Provenance:} Thomas's prolongation \cite{Thomas1926}, in the form of \cite{BEG1994}; see also \cite{Gover2010}. The sign of the $J$-term follows the sign of the Schouten tensor in the connection, and within the convention of \claimref{mass.imported-frozen-point-tractor-connection} it is the one displayed: at $w = 1$ on the constant density $1$ of an Einstein scale the display returns $(n, 0, J)$, so $\tfrac1n D\sigma = (1, 0, J/4) = (1, 0, \Lambda/6)$ in dimension four, the frozen point of Fact \claimref{mass.imported-frozen-point-tractor-connection}, a consistency the paper's own computations confirm (Lemma \claimref{mass.de-sitter-scale-frozen-point}(1), Corollary \claimref{mass.weight-polynomial-two-series}(2)). No translation between conventions is used.
mass.imported-thomas-operator.technical:
On a density $\sigma$ of conformal weight $w$ the Thomas operator gives, in the splitting of a scale $g$, $D\sigma = (w(n+2w-2)\sigma,\ (n+2w-2)\nabla_a\sigma,\ -(\Box\sigma - wJ\sigma))$, a conformally invariant tractor field of weight $w - 1$. For $w = 1$ and a scale $\sigma$, $\tfrac1n D\sigma$ is the scale tractor of $\sigma$, whose parallelism is the Einstein condition.

The sign of the $J$-term follows the sign of the Schouten tensor in the series' connection: at $w = 1$ on the constant density $1$ of an Einstein scale $\tfrac1n D\sigma$ is $(1, 0, \Lambda/6)$, the frozen point. Imported from Thomas, in the form of Bailey, Eastwood and Gover.
mass.imported-thomas-operator.lay: The Thomas operator is a standard tool of conformal geometry that turns a scale-dependent quantity into an object that does not depend on the choice of scale. Applied to a choice of scale itself, it produces the scale tractor, and an Einstein scale gives the frozen point. This classical construction is imported in the sign convention the series uses.

obj.synthesis.gtg-flat-spacetime-gauge-f.formal:
Let $V$ be the vector space of $\Cl(1,3)$, with its fixed product $a \cdot b$, $Q(a) = a^{2}$, signature $(+,-,-,-)$: \emph{flat spacetime}. Points are labelled by the position vector $x$; $\{e_\mu\}$ is a background frame with reciprocal $\{e^\mu\}$, and $\nabla = e^\mu \partial_\mu$ is the flat vector derivative. A \emph{gravitational field} on an open region of flat spacetime is a pair $(\hb, \Omega)$ of gauge fields:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] the \emph{position-gauge field} $\hb$, a position-dependent linear map of $V$, extended to multivectors as an outermorphism, with adjoint $\hb^{T}$ defined by $a \cdot \hb^{T}(b) = \hb(a) \cdot b$;
\item[(ii)] the \emph{rotation-gauge field} $\Omega$, a position-dependent linear map from vectors to bivectors.
\end{enumerate}
Its \emph{invertible region} is $U = \{x : \det \hb(x) \neq 0\}$. On $U$:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] \emph{Physical vectors.} The physical vector over a background vector $a$ is $\hb^{-1}(a)$; the frame and coframe are $g_\mu = \hb^{-1}(e_\mu)$ and $g^\mu = \hb^{T}(e^\mu)$, with $g_\mu \cdot g^\nu = \delta_\mu^\nu$. Physical vectors are compared with the flat product.
\item[(b)] \emph{Covariant derivative.} $D_a M = a \cdot \nabla M + \Omega(a) \times M$ on multivector fields, with $A \times B = \tfrac12(AB - BA)$, and $D_a \psi = a \cdot \nabla \psi + \tfrac12 \Omega(a)\psi$ on spinor fields. Along a physical vector $A$ the derivative is $A \cdot D = D_{\hb(A)}$, and the covariant vector derivative is $D = \hb^{T}(\partial_a) D_a$.
\item[(c)] \emph{Field strength.} $R(a \wedge b) = a \cdot \nabla\,\Omega(b) - b \cdot \nabla\,\Omega(a) + \Omega(a) \times \Omega(b)$, so that $[D_a, D_b]M = R(a \wedge b) \times M$. The \emph{curvature operator} is the linear map on physical bivectors $\mathcal{R}(B) = -R(\hb(B))$, the negative of the covariant field strength $R(\hb(B))$ of \cite{LDG1998}, so that the store's curvature convention holds (below); its contractions are $\mathcal{R}(b) = \partial_a \cdot \mathcal{R}(a \wedge b)$, $\mathcal{R} = \partial_a \cdot \mathcal{R}(a)$, and $\mathcal{G}(a) = \mathcal{R}(a) - \tfrac12 a\,\mathcal{R}$, the derivatives $\partial_a$ taken with respect to the physical argument.
\item[(d)] \emph{Derived metric.} $g(a, b) = \hb^{-1}(a) \cdot \hb^{-1}(b)$ for background vectors $a, b$, so $g_{\mu\nu} = g_\mu \cdot g_\nu$ and the line element is $ds^{2} = Q(\hb^{-1}(dx))$. It is a reading of $\hb$, not a structure of the background.
\item[(e)] \emph{Gauge freedoms.} For a rotor field $U$: $\hb(a) \mapsto \hb(\tilde U a U)$, equivalently $\hb^{T}(a) \mapsto U\,\hb^{T}(a)\,\tilde U$, so that physical vectors rotate, $\hb^{-1}(a) \mapsto U\,\hb^{-1}(a)\,\tilde U$; $\Omega(a) \mapsto U\,\Omega(a)\,\tilde U - 2\,(a \cdot \nabla U)\,\tilde U$, under which $\mathcal{R}(B) \mapsto U\,\mathcal{R}(\tilde U B U)\,\tilde U$. For a displacement $x \mapsto f(x)$ with differential $\underline{f}(a) = a \cdot \nabla f$: $\hb(a; x) \mapsto \underline{f}^{-1}\bigl(\hb(a; f(x))\bigr)$ and $\Omega(a; x) \mapsto \Omega(\underline{f}(a); f(x))$. The derived metric changes by the corresponding pullback and every scalar built from $\mathcal{R}$ is invariant.
\item[(f)] \emph{Field equations.} With matter stress-energy $T(a)$, a symmetric linear map on physical vectors, and cosmological constant $\Lambda$: $\mathcal{G}(a) + \Lambda a = -8\pi T(a)$, equivalently $\mathcal{R}(a) + 8\pi T(a) = (\Lambda + 4\pi\,\partial_a \cdot T(a))\,a$, and, for spinless matter, $D \wedge \hb^{T}(a) = \hb^{T}(\nabla \wedge a)$ (vanishing torsion, which fixes $\Omega$ from $\hb$).
\end{enumerate}
\emph{(d dimensions.)} The same definition on the vectors of $\Cl(p,q)$, $d = p + q \geq 3$, with the fixed product of flat $\R^{p,q}$ (the Lorentzian case $(1, d-1)$ in the sign $(+,-,\ldots,-)$), defines a gravitational field in $d$ dimensions: (a) to (f) are unchanged, the rotors being those of $\mathrm{Spin}(p,q)$, the field equation reading $\mathcal{G}(a) + \Lambda a = -8\pi G_{d}\,T(a)$, the torsion equation fixing $\Omega$ from $\hb$ as in four dimensions, and the Schouten map and Weyl curvature being $\Sch(a) = \bigl(\mathcal{R}(a) - \tfrac{a\,\mathcal{R}}{2(d-1)}\bigr)/(d-2)$ and $\mathcal{W}(a \wedge b) = \mathcal{R}(a \wedge b) - \Sch(a) \wedge b - a \wedge \Sch(b)$; de Sitter space has $\mathcal{R}(B) = \tfrac{2\Lambda}{(d-1)(d-2)}B$. The readings of Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-gtg-dictionary} that do not use the pseudoscalar (clauses (i) to (iv) and (vi), and (v) with these coefficients) are the frame formalism and hold in every dimension; the duality $\mathcal{W}(IB) = I\mathcal{W}(B)$ is four-dimensional.

The sign of $\mathcal{R}$ is the store's curvature convention, in which de Sitter space of cosmological constant $\Lambda$ has $\mathcal{R}(B) = \tfrac{\Lambda}{3}B$ and $\mathcal{R}(a) = \Lambda a$, the Ricci map is minus that of the convention in which the round sphere has positive Ricci curvature (for a physical null vector $k$ the latter is $-k \cdot \mathcal{R}(k)$), and (f) is Einstein's equation; this is the one sign flip against the literature cited: Lasenby, Doran and Gull and \cite[Ch.~14]{DoranLasenby2003} write the curvature as $R(\hb(B))$ and the field equation as $\mathcal{G}(a) - \Lambda a = 8\pi T(a)$, and a result that uses their sign says so. \emph{Note (the spin choice).} Clause (f) makes the Einstein-Cartan choice for the spin part of the matter coupling: $\Omega$ is a gauge field independent of $\hb$ (clause (ii)), and vanishing torsion is a field equation that holds for spinless matter, not an identity of the definition. Lasenby, Doran and Gull take $\hb$ and $\Omega$ as independent dynamical variables; their $\Omega$-equation with minimally coupled Dirac matter gives a torsion sourced by the spin trivector, which they identify with the torsion of the Einstein-Cartan-Sciama-Kibble theory \cite[Section 4.2, eq.~(4.37)]{LDG1998}, and with vanishing spin it is the torsion equation of (f) \cite[eq.~(4.40)]{LDG1998}. On the field space of $\Cl(2,4)$ connections preserving the frozen point this independence decides exactly the torsion equation, not the frozen point (Theorem \claimref{synthesis.frozen-point-field-space-is-the-gtg-pair-and-its-omega-equation-is-the-torsion-equation}(i)); the coupling with spin is Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-einstein-cartan-matter-coupling}. The note records a reading of the definition; the definition is unchanged.

\emph{Provenance:} Lasenby, Doran and Gull \cite{LDG1998} (Sections 3 and 4), in the series' notation, in which $\hb$ is their underbarred map and their overbarred map is $\hb^{T}$; \cite[Sections 13.4--13.6]{DoranLasenby2003}; \cite[Sections 4--5]{Lasenby2019}.
obj.synthesis.gtg-flat-spacetime-gauge-f.technical:
Gauge Theory Gravity describes gravity on flat spacetime, the vectors of $\Cl(1,3)$ with their fixed product and signature $(+,-,-,-)$. A gravitational field is a pair of gauge fields: the position-gauge field $\hb$, a position-dependent linear map on vectors, and the rotation-gauge field $\Omega(a)$, a bivector for each direction $a$. Where $\hb$ is invertible, the physical vector over a background vector $a$ is $\hb^{-1}(a)$, and the frame vectors are $g_\mu = \hb^{-1}(e_\mu)$.

The covariant derivative is $D_a M = a \cdot 
abla M + \Omega(a) 	imes M$. Its commutator gives the field strength $R(a \wedge b) = a \cdot 
abla\,\Omega(b) - b \cdot 
abla\,\Omega(a) + \Omega(a) 	imes \Omega(b)$, and the curvature operator $\mathcal{R}(B) = -R(\hb(B))$ plays the part of the Riemann tensor, with the sign of the store's curvature convention (de Sitter space has $\mathcal{R}(B) = 	frac{\Lambda}{3}B$), opposite to the gauge-theory literature's. Contracting once and twice gives the Ricci map $\mathcal{R}(b)$ and the scalar $\mathcal{R}$, and the field equations are $\mathcal{G}(a) + \Lambda a = -8\pi T(a)$ together with vanishing torsion for spinless matter. Since $\Omega$ is independent and the torsion equation is a field equation, spinning matter sources torsion: the definition makes the Einstein-Cartan choice for the spin coupling. The metric $g(a,b) = \hb^{-1}(a) \cdot \hb^{-1}(b)$ is a derived reading of $\hb$. The theory is invariant under local rotations, which rotate $\hb$ and shift $\Omega$ by a pure-gauge term, and under displacements of the background, which act by pullback. The series' $\hb$ is the map written with an underbar in Lasenby, Doran and Gull's 1998 paper, which fixes its conventions.
obj.synthesis.gtg-flat-spacetime-gauge-f.lay: In this formulation of gravity there is no curved spacetime. Spacetime is flat and fixed, and gravity is carried by two fields defined on it: one tells how directions and distances measured by physical clocks and rulers relate to the fixed background, and the other tells how local frames turn from point to point. What would be called the curvature of spacetime is the strength of the second field, just as a magnetic field is the strength of the electromagnetic potential. The usual geometric description, with its metric, can always be read off from these fields wherever the first one can be inverted.

pairing.curvature-which-loops-move-vacuu.formal:
For the Schwarzschild gravitational field on flat spacetime (Definition \claimref{obj.synthesis.gtg-flat-spacetime-gauge-fields}) and the loop spanned by physical vectors $e_{c}, e_{d}$, let $R(e_{c}, e_{d}) = R(\hb(e_{c} \wedge e_{d})) = -\mathcal{R}(e_{c} \wedge e_{d})$ be the curvature bivector, the covariant field strength on the physical plane $e_{c} \wedge e_{d}$ in the sign of \cite{LDG1998}, so that the holonomy of a small loop of area $\epsilon$ is $\exp(\epsilon R)$ to first order. In the static orthonormal frame of physical vectors the pairing classes are
\begin{gather*}
\pv(R(e_{0},e_{1})) = \pv(R(e_{2},e_{3})) = 0, \\
\pv(R(e_{0},e_{2})) = \frac{M}{r^{3}}, \qquad \pv(R(e_{1},e_{2})) = -\frac{M}{r^{3}}, \qquad \pv(R(e_{0},e_{3})) = I_5\frac{M}{r^{3}}, \qquad \pv(R(e_{1},e_{3})) = -I_5\frac{M}{r^{3}} .
\end{gather*}
The classes are numbers of $\mathrm{span}\{1, I_5\}$: the transverse null vector against which the class pairs is $m = e_{2} + I_5e_{3}$, complexified by the central pseudoscalar $I_5$ of $\Cl(2,3)$, the unit that commutes with every spacetime vector (\claimref{std-algebra.complexification-is-the-odd-extension}), and $\mb = e_{2} - I_5e_{3}$, so $\ip{m}{\mb} = -2$ (the normalisation for which the classes take the values stated).
Hence $R(\ell, e_{2}) = (M/r^{3})\,\ell e_{2}$ is a null rotation about $\ell$ with zero class, while $R(n, e_{2})$ has class $2M/r^{3}$; on the complex loops, $(\ell, m)$, $(\ell, \mb)$, $(m, \mb)$ and $(n, m)$ have zero class and $(n, \mb)$ has class $4M/r^{3}$. The holonomy therefore moves the vacuum exactly for loops with an $n \wedge \mb$ component, and for no loop lying in the null hypersurface generated by $\ell$.
pairing.curvature-which-loops-move-vacuu.technical:
For the Schwarzschild field on flat spacetime and the loop spanned by physical vectors $e_c, e_d$, the holonomy of a small loop of area $\epsilon$ is $\exp(\epsilon R(e_c, e_d))$ to first order, with $R(e_c, e_d) = -\mathcal{R}(e_c \wedge e_d)$ the field strength on the plane of the loop, and its pairing class $\pv(R(e_c, e_d))$ records whether it moves the vacuum. In the static orthonormal frame the classes vanish for the loops $(e_0, e_1)$ and $(e_2, e_3)$, and are $M/r^3$, $-M/r^3$, $I_5M/r^3$ and $-I_5M/r^3$ (numbers of $\mathrm{span}\{1, I_5\}$, the unit of the complex null vector $m = e_2 + I_5e_3$) for $(e_0, e_2)$, $(e_1, e_2)$, $(e_0, e_3)$ and $(e_1, e_3)$.

By bilinearity $R(\ell, e_2) = (M/r^3)\,\ell e_2$ is a null rotation about $\ell$ with zero class, while $R(n, e_2)$ has class $2M/r^3$; among the complex loops only $(n, \mb)$ has nonzero class, $4M/r^3$. So the holonomy moves the vacuum exactly for loops with an $n \wedge \mb$ component, and for no loop lying in the null hypersurface generated by $\ell$.
pairing.curvature-which-loops-move-vacuu.lay: Carrying the vacuum around a tiny closed loop in the gravitational field of a black hole can leave it unchanged or tilt it, depending on the loop's orientation; what tilts it is the strength of the field on the loop's plane. For Schwarzschild, loops lying in the light-like surface swept out by outgoing light rays never move the vacuum; only loops with a component along one particular ingoing complex direction do. This is a component form of the classical fact that the Schwarzschild field strength is of the simplest special algebraic type.
pairing.curvature-which-loops-move-vacuu.typing_note: The loop lemma gives only the Weyl reading, which is not part of the statement, so it moved from main to the standard-route the paper's type-D remark describes; that route also uses the lemma, which is series-proved but completion-free; the pairing-class definition went into about.

proofs.main:
The proof is in Gauge Theory Gravity on flat spacetime (Definition \claimref{obj.synthesis.gtg-flat-spacetime-gauge-fields}; the dictionary of Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-gtg-dictionary}, clauses (ii) and (iv)). Background labels $(t, r, \vartheta, \varphi)$ with background frame $e_t, e_r, e_\vartheta, e_\varphi$; the physical frame is the constant orthonormal set $e_0, e_1, e_2, e_3$ of $\Cl(1,3)$, and $e_{ab} := e_a \wedge e_b$.

\emph{The field.} The Schwarzschild field of Fact \claimref{pairing.imported-schwarzschild-connection-curvature} in the static gauge is
\[
\hb^{-1}(e_t) = \sqrt f\,e_0, \quad \hb^{-1}(e_r) = e_1/\sqrt f, \quad \hb^{-1}(e_\vartheta) = r\,e_2, \quad \hb^{-1}(e_\varphi) = r\sin\vartheta\,e_3, \qquad f = 1 - \tfrac{2M}{r},
\]
so $\hb(e_0) = e_t/\sqrt f$, $\hb(e_1) = \sqrt f\,e_r$, $\hb(e_2) = e_\vartheta/r$, $\hb(e_3) = e_\varphi/(r\sin\vartheta)$. The torsion equation $D_{e_\mu}\hb^{-1}(e_\nu) = D_{e_\nu}\hb^{-1}(e_\mu)$, with $D_a M = a\cdot\nabla M + \Omega(a)\times M$, has the unique solution
\[
\Omega(e_t) = -\tfrac{M}{r^{2}}\,e_{01}, \quad \Omega(e_r) = 0, \quad \Omega(e_\vartheta) = \sqrt f\,e_{12}, \quad \Omega(e_\varphi) = \sqrt f\sin\vartheta\,e_{13} + \cos\vartheta\,e_{23},
\]
that is $\omega(e_0) = \Omega(\hb(e_0)) = \tfrac{M}{r^{2}\sqrt f}\,e_1e_0$, $\omega(e_1) = 0$, $\omega(e_2) = \tfrac{\sqrt f}{r}\,e_{12}$, $\omega(e_3) = \tfrac{\sqrt f}{r}\,e_{13} + \tfrac{\cot\vartheta}{r}\,e_{23}$; these are the Fact's connection forms assembled into bivectors in the definition's sign. (For instance, for the pair $(t, r)$: $D_{e_r}(\sqrt f\,e_0) = \partial_r\sqrt f\,e_0 = \tfrac{M}{r^{2}\sqrt f}\,e_0$, since $\Omega(e_r) = 0$, and $D_{e_t}(e_1/\sqrt f) = \Omega(e_t)\cdot e_1/\sqrt f = -\tfrac{M}{r^{2}\sqrt f}\,e_{01}\cdot e_1 = \tfrac{M}{r^{2}\sqrt f}\,e_0$; the other five pairs are alike.)

\emph{The field strength.} $R(a \wedge b) = a\cdot\nabla\,\Omega(b) - b\cdot\nabla\,\Omega(a) + \Omega(a)\times\Omega(b)$ on the background planes. With $e_{01}\times e_{12} = -e_{02}$, $e_{01}\times e_{13} = -e_{03}$, $e_{01}\times e_{23} = 0$, $e_{12}\times e_{13} = e_{23}$, $e_{12}\times e_{23} = -e_{13}$:
\begin{gather*}
R(e_t\wedge e_r) = -\partial_r\Omega(e_t) = -\tfrac{2M}{r^{3}}\,e_{01}, \qquad
R(e_t\wedge e_\vartheta) = \Omega(e_t)\times\Omega(e_\vartheta) = \tfrac{M\sqrt f}{r^{2}}\,e_{02}, \qquad
R(e_t\wedge e_\varphi) = \tfrac{M\sqrt f\sin\vartheta}{r^{2}}\,e_{03}, \\
R(e_r\wedge e_\vartheta) = \partial_r\Omega(e_\vartheta) = \tfrac{M}{r^{2}\sqrt f}\,e_{12}, \qquad
R(e_r\wedge e_\varphi) = \tfrac{M\sin\vartheta}{r^{2}\sqrt f}\,e_{13}, \\
R(e_\vartheta\wedge e_\varphi) = \partial_\vartheta\Omega(e_\varphi) + \Omega(e_\vartheta)\times\Omega(e_\varphi) = (\sqrt f\cos\vartheta\,e_{13} - \sin\vartheta\,e_{23}) + (f\sin\vartheta\,e_{23} - \sqrt f\cos\vartheta\,e_{13}) = -\tfrac{2M}{r}\sin\vartheta\,e_{23}.
\end{gather*}
Since $\hb(e_a \wedge e_b) = \hb(e_a)\wedge\hb(e_b)$ is a multiple of the corresponding background plane, the curvature bivectors of the frame loops, $R(e_c, e_d) = R(\hb(e_c \wedge e_d)) = -\mathcal{R}(e_c \wedge e_d)$, are
\[
R(e_0, e_1) = -\tfrac{2M}{r^{3}}e_{01}, \quad R(e_2, e_3) = -\tfrac{2M}{r^{3}}e_{23}, \quad R(e_0, e_j) = \tfrac{M}{r^{3}}e_{0j}, \quad R(e_1, e_j) = \tfrac{M}{r^{3}}e_{1j} \quad (j = 2, 3):
\]
the store-sign operator $\mathcal{R}$ is diagonal on the frame planes with eigenvalue $2M/r^{3}$ on the radial plane and its dual and $-M/r^{3}$ on the four mixed planes, the spectrum the Fact states.

\emph{The classes.} The pairing class is $\pv(B) = \ip{B\cdot\ell}{m}$ (Definition \claimref{obj.pairing.pairing-class-transport}), $\ell = e_0 + e_1$, $n = e_0 - e_1$, $m = e_2 + I_5e_3$, $\mb = e_2 - I_5e_3$, with the flat product extended $\mathrm{span}\{1, I_5\}$-bilinearly ($I_5$ central in $\Cl(2,3)$), and $(a \wedge b)\cdot c = a\,(b\cdot c) - b\,(a\cdot c)$. Then $e_{01}\cdot\ell = -\ell$ and $e_{23}\cdot\ell = 0$, both orthogonal to $m$ ($\ell\cdot m = 0$), so the radial and angular loops have class $0$; $e_{02}\cdot\ell = -e_2$, $e_{12}\cdot\ell = e_2$, $e_{03}\cdot\ell = -e_3$, $e_{13}\cdot\ell = e_3$, and $e_2\cdot m = -1$, $e_3\cdot m = -I_5$, which give the classes $M/r^{3}$, $-M/r^{3}$, $I_5M/r^{3}$, $-I_5M/r^{3}$ of the statement.

\emph{The loops.} $R(u, v)$ is bilinear in $(u, v)$. For $u$ in the radial plane $\mathrm{span}(e_0, e_1)$ and $v$ in $\mathrm{span}(e_2, e_3)$, the formulas above give $R(u, v) = \tfrac{M}{r^{3}}\,u \wedge v$; on the radial plane $R(\ell, n) = -\tfrac{2M}{r^{3}}\,\ell\wedge n$, and on the angular plane $R(m, \mb) = -\tfrac{2M}{r^{3}}\,m\wedge\mb$. So $R(\ell, e_2) = \tfrac{M}{r^{3}}\,\ell e_2$ ($\ell\cdot e_2 = 0$), with $(\ell e_2)^{2} = 0$ and $(\ell e_2)\cdot\ell = 0$: a null rotation about $\ell$, of class $\tfrac{M}{r^3}\ip{(\ell\wedge e_2)\cdot\ell}{m} = 0$ since $(\ell\wedge e_2)\cdot\ell = \ell\,(e_2\cdot\ell) - e_2\,Q(\ell) = 0$. And $R(n, e_2) = \tfrac{M}{r^{3}}\,n\wedge e_2$ with $(n\wedge e_2)\cdot\ell = -2e_2$, class $2M/r^{3}$. On the complex loops, $(\ell\wedge m)\cdot\ell = (\ell\wedge\mb)\cdot\ell = (m\wedge\mb)\cdot\ell = 0$ (each factor is orthogonal to $\ell$ and $Q(\ell) = 0$), so $(\ell, m)$, $(\ell, \mb)$ and $(m, \mb)$ have class $0$; $(n\wedge m)\cdot\ell = -2m$ and $(n\wedge\mb)\cdot\ell = -2\mb$, with $\ip{m}{m} = 0$ and $\ip{\mb}{m} = -2$, so $(n, m)$ has class $0$ and $(n, \mb)$ has class $\tfrac{M}{r^{3}}\cdot 4 = 4M/r^{3}$; and $(\ell\wedge n)\cdot\ell = 2\ell$, class $0$. The six bivectors $\ell\wedge n$, $\ell\wedge m$, $\ell\wedge\mb$, $n\wedge m$, $n\wedge\mb$, $m\wedge\mb$ span the bivectors over $\mathrm{span}\{1, I_5\}$, so the class of any loop is $4M/r^{3}$ times its $n\wedge\mb$ coefficient: the holonomy moves the vacuum exactly for loops with an $n\wedge\mb$ component, and a loop in the null hypersurface generated by $\ell$ (spanned by $\ell, m, \mb$) has none. The Weyl reading of these classes is Lemma \claimref{pairing.loop-classes-are-weyl-components}.

The check computes $\Omega$ from the torsion equation of the stored field and the field strength from it on exact jets at three rational points, and compares both with the closed forms displayed here (check\_gtg\_connection\_and\_field\_strength); the classes and loops are recomputed from the displayed bivectors and from the engine's operator.

\emph{In components (the source's route).} The source derives the curvature two-forms from the connection forms of the Fact by the second structure equations, $R^{0}{}_{1} = -(f''/2)\,\theta^{0}\wedge\theta^{1}$, $R^{0}{}_{2} = R^{1}{}_{2} = -(f'/2r)\,\theta^{0}\wedge\theta^{2}, \theta^{1}\wedge\theta^{2}$, with $-f''/2 = 2M/r^{3}$ and $-f'/2r = -M/r^{3}$, and assembles them into the same bivectors.

pairing.imported-schwarzschild-connectio.formal: For the Schwarzschild gravitational field $(\hb, \Omega)$ on flat spacetime in the static gauge (Definition \claimref{obj.synthesis.gtg-flat-spacetime-gauge-fields}), with static orthonormal coframe $\theta^{0} = \sqrt f\,dt$, $\theta^{1} = dr/\sqrt f$, $\theta^{2} = r\,d\vartheta$, $\theta^{3} = r\sin\vartheta\,d\varphi$, $f = 1 - 2M/r$, the rotation-gauge field $\Omega$, read as the connection forms of that coframe, is $\omega^{0}{}_{1} = (f'/2\sqrt f)\,\theta^{0}$, $\omega^{2}{}_{1} = (\sqrt f/r)\,\theta^{2}$, $\omega^{3}{}_{1} = (\sqrt f/r)\,\theta^{3}$, $\omega^{3}{}_{2} = (\cot\vartheta/r)\,\theta^{3}$, and the curvature operator $\mathcal{R}(B)$ on physical bivectors (the field strength in the store's sign) is diagonal on the coordinate planes with eigenvalues $2M/r^{3}$ on the radial plane $\hat0\hat1$ and the angular plane $\hat2\hat3$ and $-M/r^{3}$ on the four mixed planes. The extreme eigenvalue distinguishes the pair $\{\sigma_{r}, I\sigma_{r}\}$ invariantly, the radial plane and its Hodge dual; the radial member is selected within the pair by the sign of the square, $\sigma_{r}^{2} = +1$ against $(I\sigma_{r})^{2} = -1$. Which of the two null directions of the radial plane is the vacuum's is the flag bit, which the series takes as initial data. In the Painlev\'e-Gullstrand gauge $\hb = 1 - \beta P$, $P(a) = (a \cdot e_{t})\,e_{r}$, the derived metric is $ds^{2} = dT^{2} - (dr + \beta\,dT)^{2} - r^{2}(d\vartheta^{2} + \sin^{2}\vartheta\,d\varphi^{2})$ with $\beta^{2} = 2M/r$, and $\hb$ is invertible through the horizon. \emph{Provenance:} the connection and curvature forms \cite[App.~A.2]{ButlerT5}; the pair, the sign of the square and the matching \cite[Thm.~6.1, Prop.~7.21(3)]{ButlerT5}; the Painlev\'e-Gullstrand form \cite[App.~A.1]{ButlerT5}; the flag bit \cite[Def.~2.10, Prop.~5.1]{ButlerT14}.
pairing.imported-schwarzschild-connectio.technical:
For the Schwarzschild field on flat spacetime in the static gauge, with static orthonormal coframe $\theta^0 = \sqrt f\,dt$, $\theta^1 = dr/\sqrt f$, $\theta^2 = r\,d\vartheta$, $\theta^3 = r\sin\vartheta\,d\varphi$ and $f = 1 - 2M/r$, the rotation-gauge field read as connection forms is $\omega^0{}_1 = (f'/2\sqrt f)\,\theta^0$, $\omega^2{}_1 = (\sqrt f/r)\,\theta^2$, $\omega^3{}_1 = (\sqrt f/r)\,\theta^3$ and $\omega^3{}_2 = (\cot\vartheta/r)\,\theta^3$. The curvature operator $\mathcal{R}(B)$ is diagonal on the coordinate planes, with eigenvalue $2M/r^3$ on the radial plane and the angular plane and $-M/r^3$ on the four mixed planes.

The extreme eigenvalue picks out the pair $\{\sigma_r, I\sigma_r\}$ invariantly, and the sign of the square, $\sigma_r^2 = +1$ against $(I\sigma_r)^2 = -1$, selects the radial member; which null direction of the radial plane is the vacuum's is the flag bit, taken as initial data. In the Painlev\'e-Gullstrand gauge $\hb = 1 - \beta P$ the derived metric is $ds^2 = dT^2 - (dr + \beta\,dT)^2 - r^2(d\vartheta^2 + \sin^2\vartheta\,d\varphi^2)$ with $\beta^2 = 2M/r$, and the gauge field is invertible through the horizon.
pairing.imported-schwarzschild-connectio.lay: This records the standard formulas for the gravitational field of a non-rotating black hole, described as two gauge fields on flat spacetime: how frames turn from point to point, and the field strength that plays the part of curvature, written in a frame adapted to the radius. One pair of planes, the radial one and its dual, carries the strongest field strength, which singles it out without any choice of coordinates. A second gauge, built on the clocks of infalling observers, shows that nothing goes wrong at the horizon.

pairing.imported-spin-coefficients-null-.formal:
Let $(\hb, \Omega)$ be a gravitational field on flat spacetime with covariant derivative $D$ (Definition \claimref{obj.synthesis.gtg-flat-spacetime-gauge-fields}), and $(\ell, n, m, \mb)$ a null tetrad of physical vector fields on its invertible region (complexified for $m$, $\mb$ by the central pseudoscalar $I_{5} = I_{4}e$ of the odd extension $\Cl(2,3)$, the unit that commutes with every vector, conventions U3; $\mb$ is $m$ with $I_{5} \mapsto -I_{5}$, and the coefficients are numbers of $\mathrm{span}\{1, I_{5}\}$), with $\ip{\cdot}{\cdot}$ the flat product of physical vectors, the derived metric. The four spin coefficients of the first kind are the components on $\ell, n, m, \mb$ of the linear form $X \mapsto \ip{(X \cdot D)\, \ell}{m}$, up to the normalisation of the tetrad and the sign conventions of the formalism:
\[
\kappa \leftrightarrow \ip{(\ell \cdot D)\, \ell}{m}, \qquad \tau \leftrightarrow \ip{(n \cdot D)\, \ell}{m}, \qquad \sigma \leftrightarrow \ip{(m \cdot D)\, \ell}{m}, \qquad \rho \leftrightarrow \ip{(\mb \cdot D)\, \ell}{m}
\]
(in metric language, $\ip{\nabla_X \ell}{m}$ for the Levi-Civita derivative of the derived metric).
Geometrically: $\kappa = 0$ if and only if the integral curves of $\ell$ are geodesics (worldlines along which $\ell$ is $D$-parallel up to rescaling) (this $\kappa$ is the formalism's geodesy coefficient, not the surface gravity the singularity paper writes with the same letter); $\sigma$ is the shear of the congruence of $\ell$; $\rho$ is minus its expansion (real part) and twist (imaginary part) in the standard sign convention, so that an expanding congruence has $\rho < 0$ and the radial rays of a vanishing field ($\hb = 1$, $\Omega = 0$) have $\rho = -1/r$; and $\tau$ is the rate at which $\ell$ turns transversely along $n$. The remaining eight spin coefficients are the components of $\ip{(X \cdot D)\, \ell}{n}$, $\ip{(X \cdot D)\, m}{\mb}$ and $\ip{(X \cdot D)\, n}{\mb}$: they rescale $\ell$, rotate $m$ in its plane, and tilt $n$ and $\mb$ by null rotations about $\ell$, all of which keep $\ell$ and $m$ in their span. On a Killing horizon, the locus where a Killing field $K$ is null and normal to it, the generators have $\kappa = \sigma = \rho = 0$ in any tetrad regular there. \emph{Provenance:} \cite{NewmanPenrose1962}; \cite[Ch.~4]{PenroseRindler1}; the horizon statement \cite[Sec.~12.5]{Wald1984}.
pairing.imported-spin-coefficients-null-.technical:
For a gravitational field on flat spacetime and a null tetrad $(\ell, n, m, \mb)$ of physical vectors, the four spin coefficients of the first kind are the components of the linear form $X \mapsto \ip{(X \cdot D)\,\ell}{m}$, with $D$ the covariant derivative and the flat product of physical vectors: $\kappa$, $\tau$, $\sigma$, $\rho$ correspond to $X = \ell, n, m, \mb$, up to normalisation and sign conventions. $\kappa = 0$ exactly when the integral curves of $\ell$ are geodesics, $\sigma$ is the shear, $\rho$ is minus the expansion (real part) and twist (imaginary part), so that radial rays with no gravitational field have $\rho = -1/r$, and $\tau$ is the rate at which $\ell$ turns transversely along $n$.

The other eight coefficients rescale $\ell$, rotate $m$ in its plane, and tilt $n$ and $\mb$ by null rotations about $\ell$, all keeping $\ell$ and $m$ in their span. On a Killing horizon the generators have $\kappa = \sigma = \rho = 0$ in any tetrad regular there. Imported from Newman and Penrose, Penrose and Rindler, and Wald.
pairing.imported-spin-coefficients-null-.lay: The Newman-Penrose spin coefficients are a standard set of numbers describing how a family of light rays bends, spreads, shears and twists as it travels. Four of them measure how the ray direction tilts out of its plane; the others only relabel it. On a black hole horizon the light rays that make up the horizon neither bend, shear nor spread.

pairing.imported-weyl-scalars-petrov-typ.formal: For a gravitational field $(\hb, \Omega)$ on flat spacetime (Definition \claimref{obj.synthesis.gtg-flat-spacetime-gauge-fields}) and a null tetrad $(\ell, n, m, \mb)$ of physical vectors, the Weyl map $\mathcal{W}$ of the field strength, read as the Weyl tensor $C$ of the derived metric on the tetrad's bivectors $\ell \wedge m$, $\ell \wedge n$ and $n \wedge \mb$, has five complex components, numbers of $\mathrm{span}\{1, I_{5}\}$ since $m$ and $\mb$ are complexified by the central pseudoscalar $I_{5} = I_{4}e$ of the odd extension (conventions U3), $\Psi_{0} = C(\ell, m, \ell, m)$, $\Psi_{1} = C(\ell, n, \ell, m)$, $\Psi_{2} = C(\ell, m, \mb, n)$, $\Psi_{3} = C(\ell, n, \mb, n)$, $\Psi_{4} = C(n, \mb, n, \mb)$, up to normalisation and sign convention; $\ell$ is a principal null direction if and only if $\Psi_{0} = 0$ and a repeated one if and only if $\Psi_{0} = \Psi_{1} = 0$. The Schwarzschild field is of Petrov type D with the outgoing and ingoing radial null directions as its repeated principal directions, $\Psi_{2} = -M/r^{3}$ in the unit-normalised tetrad and all other $\Psi$ zero. For a vacuum field, $\mathcal{R}(a) = 0$ (Ricci-flat), the curvature operator is its Weyl map, $\mathcal{R} = \mathcal{W}$. \emph{Provenance:} \cite[Ch.~8]{PenroseRindler2}; \cite{NewmanPenrose1962}.
pairing.imported-weyl-scalars-petrov-typ.technical:
For a gravitational field on flat spacetime and a null tetrad $(\ell, n, m, \mb)$ of physical vectors, the Weyl map of the field strength (the Weyl tensor of the derived metric) has five complex components $\Psi_0, \dots, \Psi_4$, for instance $\Psi_0 = C(\ell, m, \ell, m)$ and $\Psi_2 = C(\ell, m, \mb, n)$, up to normalisation and sign convention. The direction $\ell$ is principal if and only if $\Psi_0 = 0$, and repeated principal if and only if $\Psi_0 = \Psi_1 = 0$.

The Schwarzschild field is of Petrov type D, its repeated principal directions being the outgoing and ingoing radial null directions, with $\Psi_2 = -M/r^3$ in the unit-normalised tetrad and all other $\Psi$ zero. For a vacuum field, $\mathcal{R}(a) = 0$, the curvature operator is its Weyl map. Imported from Penrose and Rindler and from Newman and Penrose.
pairing.imported-weyl-scalars-petrov-typ.lay: The part of the gravitational field strength that describes tidal forces and gravitational waves can be summarised by five complex numbers relative to a frame of light-like directions. Black holes like Schwarzschild are especially simple: in the natural frame only one of the five is nonzero, and the radial light rays are the field strength's special directions. This standard result is imported.

pairing.loop-classes-are-weyl-components.formal:
For a vacuum gravitational field on flat spacetime, $\mathcal{R}(a) = 0$ (Ricci-flat; Definition \claimref{obj.synthesis.gtg-flat-spacetime-gauge-fields}), let $R(u, v) = R(\hb(u \wedge v)) = -\mathcal{R}(u \wedge v)$ be the curvature bivector of the loop $(u, v)$ of physical vectors, the covariant field strength on the plane $u \wedge v$, and write
\[
C(u, v, w, z) := \ip{R(u, v)\cdot w}{z},
\]
with the flat product of physical vectors, so that the class of the loop $(u, v)$ is $C(u, v, \ell, m)$. The six loops of the null tetrad then have classes
\[
(\ell, m) : \Psi_{0}, \quad (\ell, \mb) : 0, \quad (m, \mb) : -\Psi_{1}, \quad (\ell, n) : \Psi_{1}, \quad (n, m) : 0, \quad (n, \mb) : -\Psi_{2},
\]
up to the tetrad's normalisation. Hence every loop in the null cone of $\ell$ has zero class if and only if $\Psi_{0} = \Psi_{1} = 0$, that is, if and only if $\ell$ is a repeated principal null direction; the radial loop then has zero class as well, and only $\Psi_{2}$ remains.
pairing.loop-classes-are-weyl-components.technical:
For a vacuum gravitational field on flat spacetime set $C(u, v, w, z) = \ip{R(u, v)\cdot w}{z}$, with $R(u, v) = -\mathcal{R}(u \wedge v)$ the field strength on the plane of the loop, so that the class of the loop $(u, v)$ is $C(u, v, \ell, m)$. From the definitions of the Weyl scalars, the pair symmetry and the tracelessness of $C$ in the null tetrad, the six tetrad loops have classes $(\ell, m): \Psi_0$, $(\ell, \mb): 0$, $(m, \mb): -\Psi_1$, $(\ell, n): \Psi_1$, $(n, m): 0$ and $(n, \mb): -\Psi_2$, up to the tetrad's normalisation.

Hence every loop in the null cone of $\ell$ has zero class if and only if $\Psi_0 = \Psi_1 = 0$, that is, if and only if $\ell$ is a repeated principal null direction; the radial loop then has zero class as well, and only $\Psi_2$ remains.
pairing.loop-classes-are-weyl-components.lay: Whether carrying the vacuum around a small loop moves it can be read directly off the standard components of the tidal part of the gravitational field strength. Loops lying in the light cone of the vacuum's direction leave it unmoved exactly when that direction is one of the curvature's doubly special directions. In that case only one component of the field strength can move the vacuum.

proofs.main:
The proof is in Gauge Theory Gravity: for a vacuum field the curvature operator is its Weyl part, $\mathcal{R} = \mathcal{W}$, a linear map on physical bivectors that is symmetric, $\langle A\,\mathcal{W}(B)\rangle_{0} = \langle\mathcal{W}(A)\,B\rangle_{0}$ (the pair symmetry of the Riemann tensor, which $\mathcal{R}$ reads by clause (iv) of Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-gtg-dictionary}; in geometric algebra a consequence of the first Bianchi identity $\partial_{a}\wedge\mathcal{R}(a\wedge b) = 0$), and trace-free, $\partial_{a}\cdot\mathcal{W}(a \wedge b) = 0$ (clause (v) of that Fact); the null tetrad and the Weyl scalars are those of Fact \claimref{pairing.imported-weyl-scalars-petrov-type-schwarzschild}, $\Psi_{0} = C(\ell, m, \ell, m)$, $\Psi_{1} = C(\ell, n, \ell, m)$, $\Psi_{2} = C(\ell, m, \mb, n)$, with the flat product of physical vectors extended bilinearly over the complex unit of $m$.

\emph{$C$ as a bilinear form of the Weyl map.} For a bivector $B$ and vectors $w, z$, $(B\cdot w)\cdot z = B\cdot(w \wedge z) := \langle B\,(w\wedge z)\rangle_{0}$ (for $B = a \wedge b$ both sides are $(a\cdot z)(b\cdot w) - (a\cdot w)(b\cdot z)$). Hence
\[
C(u, v, w, z) = R(u, v)\cdot(w \wedge z) = -\,\mathcal{W}(u \wedge v)\cdot(w \wedge z).
\]
So $C$ is antisymmetric in $(u, v)$ and in $(w, z)$, and the symmetry of $\mathcal{W}$ gives the pair symmetry $C(u, v, w, z) = C(w, z, u, v)$.

\emph{The trace in the null tetrad.} For any frame $\{f_{a}\}$ with reciprocal frame $\{f^{a}\}$, $\partial_{a} = \sum_{a} f^{a}\,(f_{a}\cdot\partial)$, and for a vector $c$ and bivector $B$, $(c\cdot B)\cdot v = -B\cdot(c \wedge v)$. So
\[
0 \;=\; v\cdot\bigl(\partial_{a}\cdot\mathcal{W}(a \wedge u)\bigr) \;=\; \sum_{a} C(f_{a}, u, f^{a}, v) .
\]
For the tetrad $\ell, n, m, \mb$ with $\ell\cdot n = 2$, $m\cdot\mb = -2$ and the other products zero, the reciprocal frame is $\ell \mapsto n/2$, $n \mapsto \ell/2$, $m \mapsto -\mb/2$, $\mb \mapsto -m/2$, and the trace condition reads
\[
\tfrac12\bigl[C(\ell, u, n, v) + C(n, u, \ell, v)\bigr] - \tfrac12\bigl[C(m, u, \mb, v) + C(\mb, u, m, v)\bigr] = 0 \qquad (\mathrm{T}_{u,v})
\]
for all $u, v$ (for another normalisation of the tetrad the coefficients scale accordingly).

\emph{The six classes.} The class of the loop $(u, v)$ is $C(u, v, \ell, m)$. The loops $(\ell, m)$ and $(\ell, n)$ give $\Psi_{0}$ and $\Psi_{1}$ by definition. The loop $(n, \mb)$ gives $C(n, \mb, \ell, m) = C(\ell, m, n, \mb) = -C(\ell, m, \mb, n) = -\Psi_{2}$, by the pair symmetry and the antisymmetry in the last pair. In $(\mathrm{T}_{\ell, \ell})$ the two $\ell$-terms vanish by antisymmetry, so $C(m, \ell, \mb, \ell) = -C(\mb, \ell, m, \ell)$, while the pair symmetry makes them equal; hence both vanish, and $C(\ell, \mb, \ell, m) = C(\ell, m, \ell, \mb) = C(m, \ell, \mb, \ell) = 0$. $(\mathrm{T}_{m, \ell})$ leaves $C(\ell, m, n, \ell) = C(\mb, m, m, \ell)$; the left side is $-C(\ell, m, \ell, n) = -C(\ell, n, \ell, m) = -\Psi_{1}$ and the right side is $C(m, \mb, \ell, m)$, so the loop $(m, \mb)$ has class $-\Psi_{1}$. $(\mathrm{T}_{m, m})$ leaves $C(\ell, m, n, m) + C(n, m, \ell, m) = 0$, and the two terms are equal by the pair symmetry, so the loop $(n, m)$ has class $0$.

\emph{The equivalence.} The loops in the null cone of $\ell$ are the combinations of $(\ell, m)$, $(\ell, \mb)$ and $(m, \mb)$, with classes $\Psi_{0}$, $0$, $-\Psi_{1}$; they all vanish exactly when $\Psi_{0} = \Psi_{1} = 0$, which by the Fact is the condition that $\ell$ is a repeated principal null direction. Then the radial loop $(\ell, n)$ has class $\Psi_{1} = 0$, and of the six only $(n, \mb)$, with $-\Psi_{2}$, can be nonzero.

The check computes, on all ten basis Weyl maps of $\Cl(1,3)$ and on a generic operator, the identity $(B\cdot w)\cdot z = B\cdot(w \wedge z)$, the reciprocal-frame form of the trace (it equals $v\cdot(\partial_{a}\cdot X(a \wedge u))$ for every bivector map $X$, Weyl or not, and vanishes on the Weyl maps) and the pair symmetry, and then the six identities, both in the adapted tetrad and in the unit-normalised one (check\_gtg\_trace\_and\_pair\_symmetry); the earlier functions verify the table on the Weyl space and on the Schwarzschild operator.

\emph{In components.} The same argument in an orthonormal frame is the source's: the trace is $\eta^{ab}C(e_{a}, u, e_{b}, v) = 0$, written in the null tetrad as $(\mathrm{T}_{u,v})$ up to the normalisation.

singularity.imported-equivalence-einstei.formal: On any region where $\hb$ is invertible, the GTG field equations for $(\hb, \Omega)$ (Definition \claimref{obj.synthesis.gtg-flat-spacetime-gauge-fields}(f)) are equivalent to the Einstein field equations for the derived metric $g(a,b) = \hb^{-1}(a)\cdot\hb^{-1}(b)$ (the Definition's clause (d)); in vacuum, to Ricci-flatness of $g$. Moreover the curvatures correspond, not only the equations: on the invertible region the GTG curvature operator $B \mapsto \mathcal{R}(B)$ on physical bivectors is the curvature of $g$ (in components: $\mathcal{R}(g_\mu \wedge g_\nu)$, on the coordinate planes of the frame $g_\mu = \hb^{-1}(e_\mu)$ and contracted with the reciprocal planes $g^\rho \wedge g^\sigma$, is the Riemann tensor $R_{\mu\nu}{}^{\rho\sigma}$ of $g$), so the curvature operator on bivectors, its spectrum, its eigenplanes and its scalar invariants are the same objects in the two pictures. \emph{Provenance:} Lasenby, Doran and Gull \cite[\S 4.3 and App.~C]{LDG1998}; textbook form, including the dictionary between $\mathcal{R}(B)$ and the Riemann tensor, \cite[Ch.~13-14]{DoranLasenby2003}. It is the second clause that licenses the assembly of Theorem \claimref{singularity.curvature-gauge-field-exact-shape-decoupling}'s spectrum from the two formalisms.
singularity.imported-equivalence-einstei.technical:
On any region where $\hb$ is invertible, the gauge-theory field equations for $(\hb, \Omega)$ are equivalent to the Einstein field equations for the induced metric, and in vacuum to Ricci-flatness of $g$. The correspondence extends to curvature: the gauge-theory curvature operator $\mathcal{R}(B)$ on physical bivectors is the curvature of $g$, its values on the frame planes $g_\mu \wedge g_\nu$, $g_\mu = \hb^{-1}(e_\mu)$, giving the Riemann components of $g$.

So the curvature operator on bivectors, its spectrum, eigenplanes and scalar invariants are the same objects in both pictures, which is what allows a curvature spectrum to be assembled from computations in the two formalisms. The result is imported from the literature on gauge-theory gravity.
singularity.imported-equivalence-einstei.lay: Gravity can be described either as the curvature of spacetime, as in Einstein's theory, or as a gauge theory on flat spacetime written in geometric algebra. This imported result says that wherever the gauge field is invertible the two descriptions have equivalent field equations and the same curvature. Curvature calculations can therefore be done in either language and combined.

standard-model.imported-tractor-bundle-s.formal: Over the invertible region of a gravitational field $(\hb, \Omega)$ on flat spacetime (Definition \claimref{obj.synthesis.gtg-flat-spacetime-gauge-fields}), with the conformal class of its derived metric, the standard tractor bundle has rank six, fibre the vectors of $\Cl(2,4)$, carries a metric of signature $(2,4)$, and carries a canonical connection depending only on the conformal class, preserving that metric, which on flat spacetime is the rotation-gauge field of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.gtg-tractor-gauge-field-reproduces-tractor-connection}; its structure group is $SO(2,4)$. Where the conformal manifold is spin, which is assumed throughout (as the correspondence paper assumes it; the invertible region, an open subset of flat spacetime, is), its spinor bundle is the bundle of conformal spinors (the local twistor bundle), of rank four over the complex unit $I_6$, with fibre $\CS$, on whose fibres the ascended algebra $\Cl(2,4)$ acts with the conformal spinors (twistors) of Fact \claimref{standard-model.imported-pair-systems-two-chirality-halves} as fibre elements; the conformal spinor connection (local twistor transport) is the spinor connection induced by the tractor connection, and its structure group is $\mathrm{Spin}(2,4)$, with Lie algebra $\mathfrak{so}(2,4)$. \emph{Provenance:} the connection formula, \cite[Fact~4.1]{ButlerT6}; the rank, the signature, the structure group and the spinor bundle, \cite[Fact~4.9, Prop.~4.10]{ButlerT9}.
standard-model.imported-tractor-bundle-s.technical:
Over the invertible region of a gravitational field on flat spacetime, with the conformal class of its derived metric, the standard tractor bundle has rank six (fibre the vectors of $\Cl(2,4)$), a metric of signature $(2,4)$, and a canonical metric-preserving connection depending only on the conformal class, on flat spacetime the tractor gauge field, with structure group $SO(2,4)$. Where the manifold is spin, as assumed throughout, its spinor bundle is the rank-four bundle of conformal spinors, on whose fibres $\Cl(2,4)$ acts with conformal spinors as fibre elements.

The conformal spinor connection is the spinor connection induced by the tractor connection, with structure group $\mathrm{Spin}(2,4)$ and Lie algebra $\mathfrak{so}(2,4)$. The entry restates the series' tractor connection formula and its identification of the spinor bundle with the bundle of conformal spinors.
standard-model.imported-tractor-bundle-s.lay: On spacetime considered up to rescaling there is a natural six-component structure with a way of carrying it from point to point, and, assuming spacetime is spin (as the series does throughout), an associated four-component structure whose elements are spinors of the conformal geometry. The second is carried around by the transport induced from the first. These facts, restated from earlier in the series, are the geometric setting for its particle content.

Read in Gauge Theory Gravity: the metric $g$ below is the derived metric of the gravitational field $(\hb, \Omega)$ on flat spacetime, the manifold is the invertible region, and the tractor connection is the flat-space $\Cl(2,4)$ gauge field of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.gtg-tractor-gauge-field-reproduces-tractor-connection}; the index computation below is its reading in the splitting of $g$ (Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-gtg-dictionary}).

Over a conformal four-manifold the standard tractor bundle has rank six, carries a metric of signature $(2,4)$, and carries a canonical connection depending only on the conformal class, preserving that metric; its structure group is $SO(2,4)$. Where the conformal manifold is spin, which is assumed throughout (as the correspondence paper assumes it), its spinor bundle is the bundle of conformal spinors (the local twistor bundle), of rank four over the complex unit $I_6$, with fibre $\CS$, on whose fibres the ascended algebra $\Cl(2,4)$ acts with the conformal spinors (twistors) of Fact \claimref{standard-model.imported-pair-systems-two-chirality-halves} as fibre elements; the conformal spinor connection (local twistor transport) is the spinor connection induced by the tractor connection, and its structure group is $\mathrm{Spin}(2,4)$, with Lie algebra $\mathfrak{so}(2,4)$. \emph{Provenance:} the connection formula, \cite[Fact~4.1]{ButlerT6} (\claimref{interior.imported-tractor-connection}); the rank, the signature, the structure group and the spinor bundle, \cite[Fact~4.9, Prop.~4.10]{ButlerT9} (\claimref{correspondence.local-twistor-transport-ascended-spinor-connection}, \claimref{correspondence.imported-tractor-connection-local-twistor-transport}).
