synthesis.imported-conformal-gravity-bac.technical: Conformal (Weyl) gravity takes as action the integral of the square of the Weyl tensor, the part of the curvature that is unchanged by local rescalings of lengths. Bach found its field equations: they involve four derivatives of the metric, and every solution of Einstein's equations in four dimensions solves them, whatever the cosmological constant, as does every metric conformal to one; they have further solutions. Kaku, Townsend and van Nieuwenhuizen obtained the same action as a gauge theory of the conformal group: with the torsion set to zero and the special-conformal gauge field expressed through the curvature, the alternating square of the conformal field strength is the Weyl square. In the series the conformal group acts on $\Cl(2,4)$ and its gauge field is the tractor gauge field. Taken from the literature.
synthesis.imported-conformal-gravity-bac.lay: Einstein's theory is not the only possible law of gravity. One alternative, Weyl gravity, cares only about the shape of spacetime and not its size; Bach worked out its equations, which are more complicated than Einstein's but are satisfied by every solution of Einstein's. Later physicists showed that it is exactly what one gets by treating the symmetries of shape-preserving maps as a force field. These are results taken from the literature.

imported_from.citation: R. Bach, Zur Weylschen Relativitaetstheorie und der Weylschen Erweiterung des Kruemmungstensorbegriffs, Math. Z. 9 (1921), 110--135.
M. Kaku, P. K. Townsend and P. van Nieuwenhuizen, Gauge theory of the conformal and superconformal group, Phys. Lett. B 69 (1977), 304--308.

synthesis.imported-einstein-cartan-matte.formal:
Units $\hbar = c = 1$; store sign (Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-gtg-dictionary}): signature $(+,-,-,-)$ on the physical vectors, de Sitter curvature $\mathcal{R}(B) = \tfrac{\Lambda}{3}B$. Let $(\hb, \Omega)$ be a gravitational field on flat spacetime (Definition \claimref{obj.synthesis.gtg-flat-spacetime-gauge-fields}), with $\hb$ (the frame) and $\Omega$ (the rotation gauge field, equivalently the spin connection) varied independently, and let the gravitational functional be the Einstein-Cartan functional with cosmological term, normalised by Newton's constant $G$. Add a matter functional $S_{m}[\hb, \Omega, \psi]$ coupled minimally (through the covariant derivative built from $\hb$ and $\Omega$).
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] (Frame equation.) The frame variation of $S_{m}$ defines the energy-momentum map $T(a)$ of the matter, and the frame equation is $\mathcal{G}(a) + \Lambda a + 8\pi G\,T(a) = 0$, with $\mathcal{G}$ the Einstein map of the field strength.
\item[(b)] (Connection equation.) The variation of $\Omega$ fixes the torsion algebraically in terms of the spin density of the matter: it vanishes where the spin density vanishes, and for a Dirac field minimal coupling gives a unique spin-torsion interaction, its spin trivector sourcing a totally antisymmetric torsion.
\item[(c)] (Torsion-free case.) For matter with no spin density (a perfect fluid, a minimally coupled scalar) the connection is the torsion-free one and (a) is Einstein's equation with cosmological constant and source $T$, the symmetric energy-momentum map.
\end{enumerate}
\emph{Provenance:} \cite{Kibble1961, Sciama1964, HehlEtAl1976, LasenbyDoranGull1998}.
synthesis.imported-einstein-cartan-matte.technical: When the gravitational field is treated as a gauge field, as in the Einstein-Cartan theory of Kibble and Sciama and in Gauge Theory Gravity, the frame and the connection are independent fields. Matter is coupled by putting the connection into its derivatives. Varying the frame then gives Einstein's equations with the matter's energy-momentum as source and Newton's constant as the overall normalisation; varying the connection ties the torsion to the matter's spin density, so torsion is absent where matter carries no spin, and for a Dirac field minimal coupling fixes the form of the spin-torsion interaction. Hehl, von der Heyde, Kerlick and Nester review the theory as a gauge theory of the Poincare group; Lasenby, Doran and Gull give it in geometric algebra on flat spacetime. Taken from the literature, with the field equation written in the store's sign.
synthesis.imported-einstein-cartan-matte.lay: Einstein's theory says how matter curves spacetime. When gravity is described as a gauge field, like the fields of particle physics, there is a standard way to let matter act as its source: the matter's energy and momentum appear in Einstein's equations, and the matter's spin produces a tiny extra twisting of spacetime, called torsion, that vanishes where there is no spin. This is the standard coupling, taken from the literature.

imported_from.citation: T. W. B. Kibble, Lorentz invariance and the gravitational field, J. Math. Phys. 2 (1961), 212--221.
D. W. Sciama, The physical structure of general relativity, Rev. Mod. Phys. 36 (1964), 463--469.
F. W. Hehl, P. von der Heyde, G. D. Kerlick and J. M. Nester, General relativity with spin and torsion: foundations and prospects, Rev. Mod. Phys. 48 (1976), 393--416.
A. N. Lasenby, C. J. L. Doran and S. F. Gull, Gravity, gauge theories and geometric algebra, Phil. Trans. R. Soc. Lond. A 356 (1998), 487--582.

synthesis.imported-five-dimensional-cher.formal:
Let $A$ be a gauge field on a five-dimensional region with values in the bivectors of a six-dimensional Clifford algebra ($\Cl(2,4)$, the anti-de Sitter case in five dimensions, or $\Cl(1,5)$), with field strength $F$, and let $P(F_{1}, F_{2}, F_{3})$ be the cubic invariant, the pseudoscalar part of $F_{1} \wedge F_{2} \wedge F_{3}$ (index reading $\epsilon_{ABCDEF}F_{1}^{AB}F_{2}^{CD}F_{3}^{EF}$).
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] (The action.) Five-dimensional Chern-Simons gravity is $\kappa_{5}\int\mathrm{CS}_{5}(A)$, with $\mathrm{CS}_{5}$ the Chern-Simons form of $P$, $d\,\mathrm{CS}_{5}(A) = P(F, F, F)$, and constant $\kappa_{5}$ (the level). It needs no metric and no reduction datum, and is gauge invariant up to boundary terms; its field equations are $P(J, F, F) = 0$ for every bivector $J$.
\item[(b)] (The Lovelock form.) Splitting $A = \omega + E$ by a fixed vector $V$ of nonzero square, with $\omega$ in the stabiliser of $V$ (its curvature $R$) and $E = \theta \wedge V/Q(V)$ carrying the frame $\theta$, the Chern-Simons form is, up to exact forms and torsion terms, a constant times the combination of the five-dimensional Lovelock densities $\epsilon(R, R, \theta) + \tfrac23\ell^{-2}\epsilon(R, \theta, \theta, \theta) + \tfrac15\ell^{-4}\epsilon(\theta, \theta, \theta, \theta, \theta)$, with $\ell^{2} = |Q(V)|$ the (anti-)de Sitter radius (index reading $\epsilon_{abcde}(R^{ab}R^{cd}e^{e} + \tfrac23\ell^{-2}R^{ab}e^{c}e^{d}e^{e} + \tfrac15\ell^{-4}e^{a}e^{b}e^{c}e^{d}e^{e})$): the Euler (Gauss-Bonnet), Einstein-Hilbert and volume terms with ratios fixed by gauge invariance.
\end{enumerate}
\emph{Note (reduction along a line; standard, from the literature).} On a product of a four-dimensional region with a line, with the frame along the line a multiple of $dy$, each five-dimensional Lovelock density reduces to $dy$ wedged with the four-dimensional density of the same type, with multiplicities fixed by the choice of the frame leg along $dy$; this is how a five-dimensional Chern-Simons form yields a four-dimensional curvature-squared density.

\emph{Provenance:} \cite{Chamseddine1989, Chamseddine1990}; the transgression form and the Lovelock expansion as in \cite{Zanelli2005}.
synthesis.imported-five-dimensional-cher.technical: In five dimensions gravity can be written as a Chern-Simons theory of the conformal (anti-de Sitter) group: the action is the Chern-Simons form of the cubic invariant of its gauge field, needs no metric, and is gauge invariant up to boundary terms. Chamseddine showed that, once a vector splits the gauge field into a connection and a frame, the action becomes a definite combination of the Gauss-Bonnet, Einstein-Hilbert and cosmological terms, with relative weights $1$, $\tfrac23\ell^{-2}$ and $\tfrac15\ell^{-4}$ fixed by the larger gauge invariance, $\ell$ the radius. Reducing such densities along a line in the standard Kaluza-Klein way gives four-dimensional curvature-squared densities. Taken from the literature; in the series the gauge field takes values in the bivectors of $\Cl(2,4)$.
synthesis.imported-five-dimensional-cher.lay: In a five-dimensional world, gravity can be built entirely from the symmetries of spacetime, with no lengths put in by hand; Chamseddine found that the rule then contains the usual ingredients of gravity in fixed proportions. Shrinking one direction to a line gives four-dimensional rules of a related form. This is taken from the literature.

imported_from.citation: A. H. Chamseddine, Topological gauge theory of gravity in five and all odd dimensions, Phys. Lett. B 233 (1989), 291--294.
A. H. Chamseddine, Topological gravity and supergravity in various dimensions, Nucl. Phys. B 346 (1990), 213--234.
J. Zanelli, Lecture notes on Chern-Simons (super-)gravities, arXiv:hep-th/0502193 (second edition, 2008).

synthesis.imported-gauss-bonnet-with-cor.formal:
Let $P$ be a compact oriented surface with piecewise smooth edge $\partial P$ and a Riemannian metric, with Gauss curvature $K$, area element $dA$, and Euler characteristic $\chi(P)$; in the series $P$ is a patch of a spacelike two-surface in the invertible region of a gravitational field $(\hb, \Omega)$ on flat spacetime (Definition \claimref{obj.synthesis.gtg-flat-spacetime-gauge-fields}), such as a cut of a horizon, with the Riemannian metric $-h$, $h$ the metric that the derived metric induces.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] (Gauss-Bonnet with edge and corners.) $\int_{P}K\,dA + \oint_{\partial P}k_{g}\,ds + \sum_{j}\varepsilon_{j} = 2\pi\chi(P)$, with $k_{g}$ the geodesic curvature of the edge taken with respect to the inward normal and $\varepsilon_{j}$ the exterior turning angles at its corners. Locally, for an orthonormal coframe $(e^{2}, e^{3})$ with rotation one-form $\omega$, $d\omega = K\,e^{2} \wedge e^{3}$, so $\int_{P}K\,dA = \oint_{\partial P}\omega$ for a frame smooth on $P$.
\item[(b)] (Poincare-Hopf and clutching.) A tangent vector field with isolated zeros on a closed surface $\Sigma$ has indices summing to $\chi(\Sigma)$; in particular a sphere ($\chi = 2$) carries no nowhere-vanishing tangent field and no smooth tangent frame. Cutting the sphere along a circle into two caps with tangent frames smooth on each, the rotation relating the two frames along the circle winds $\chi(S^{2}) = 2$ times (the clutching number of its tangent bundle).
\item[(c)] (The two-dimensional Gibbons-Hawking term.) For a functional of the metric with Einstein-Hilbert density, a region with edge needs the edge term $2\oint k\,ds$, $k$ the trace of the extrinsic curvature of the edge (the Gibbons-Hawking, or York, term), for its variational principle to be well posed with the edge metric held fixed. On a surface the extrinsic curvature of the edge is its geodesic curvature, so the two-dimensional term is $2\oint_{\partial P}k_{g}\,ds$, and by (a) the two-dimensional Einstein-Hilbert functional with it, $\int_{P}{}^{(2)}\!R\,dA + 2\oint_{\partial P}k_{g}\,ds$ with ${}^{(2)}\!R = 2K$, equals $4\pi\chi(P) - 2\sum_{j}\varepsilon_{j}$, a topological constant.
\end{enumerate}
\emph{Beyond one flat chart.} The Euler characteristic of a closed surface in (b) and the clutching of two caps are global: they are read on the surface assembled from charts of flat spacetime, each with its own gravitational field, glued by gauge transformations; (a) on a patch with a smooth frame and (c) are local.

\emph{Provenance:} \cite[Sec.~4-5]{doCarmo1976} for (a); \cite{Hopf1927} for the index theorem and \cite{MilnorStasheff1974} for the clutching description in (b); \cite{York1972, GibbonsHawking1977} for the edge term in (c).
synthesis.imported-gauss-bonnet-with-cor.technical: Three classical facts about surfaces. Gauss-Bonnet for a patch with an edge: the total curvature inside, plus the total turning of the edge measured by its geodesic curvature, plus the turning angles at its corners, is $2\pi$ times the Euler characteristic of the patch; locally the curvature is the exterior derivative of the frame's rotation form, so the curvature inside equals the frame's rotation around the edge. Poincare and Hopf: on a closed surface the zeros of any tangent field, counted with their indices, add up to the Euler characteristic, so the sphere has no smooth tangent frame, and two frames smooth on two caps differ along the dividing circle by a rotation winding twice. Gibbons, Hawking and York: an action with the Einstein-Hilbert density needs a boundary term, twice the integral of the trace of the boundary's extrinsic curvature, to have a good variational principle; on a surface this term is twice the edge's geodesic curvature, and with it the two-dimensional action is topological. Taken from the literature.
synthesis.imported-gauss-bonnet-with-cor.lay: However a patch of surface is curved, its total curvature plus the bending of its edge and the turns at its corners always add up to a fixed amount set by how many holes it has. A related fact says that on a sphere any arrangement of arrows tangent to the surface must have somewhere a point where it fails, the hairy-ball theorem. And the standard extra edge term of Einstein's action principle, on a surface, is exactly the edge's bending that makes the total fixed. These are classical results taken from the literature.

imported_from.citation: M. P. do Carmo, Differential Geometry of Curves and Surfaces, Prentice-Hall, Englewood Cliffs (1976).
H. Hopf, Vektorfelder in n-dimensionalen Mannigfaltigkeiten, Math. Ann. 96 (1927), 225--249.
J. W. Milnor and J. D. Stasheff, Characteristic Classes, Annals of Mathematics Studies 76, Princeton University Press (1974).

synthesis.imported-gtg-dictionary.formal:
Let $(\hb, \Omega)$ be a gravitational field on flat spacetime with invertible region $U$ and derived metric $g$ (Definition \claimref{obj.synthesis.gtg-flat-spacetime-gauge-fields}), with frame $g_\mu = \hb^{-1}(e_\mu)$ and coframe $g^\mu = \hb^{T}(e^\mu)$. On $U$, with $\Omega$ the torsion-free field of $\hb$:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] \emph{Vectors.} The tangent vectors of $(U, g)$ at $x$ are the physical vectors $\hb^{-1}(a)$, and $g(a,b) = \hb^{-1}(a) \cdot \hb^{-1}(b)$. A background vector $a$ is null, timelike or spacelike for $g$ exactly when $Q(\hb^{-1}(a))$ is zero, positive or negative; the light cone of $g$ at $x$ is the image under $\hb$ of the null cone of the flat product. The components of a physical vector field $A$ are $A^\mu = g^\mu \cdot A$, and an orthonormal frame of $g$ is any orthonormal set $\{\gamma_a\}$ of $\Cl(1,3)$, with tetrad components $\gamma^a \cdot g_\mu$.
\item[(ii)] \emph{Levi-Civita derivative and parallel transport.} The Levi-Civita derivative of a physical vector field $A$ along $e_\mu$ is $D_{e_\mu} A$ (in components: $\nabla_\mu A^\nu = g^\nu \cdot D_{e_\mu} A$, and the Christoffel symbols are $\Gamma^\rho{}_{\mu\nu} = g^\rho \cdot D_{e_\mu} g_\nu$). Parallel transport along a curve $x(\lambda)$ is $D_{x'} M = 0$; it is solved by $M(\lambda) = U M(0) \tilde U$ with $dU/d\lambda = -\tfrac12\Omega(x')U$, $U(0) = 1$, a rotor, so it preserves the flat product of physical vectors.
\item[(iii)] \emph{Geodesics.} A curve $x(\tau)$ is an affinely parametrised timelike (null) geodesic of $g$ exactly when $v = \hb^{-1}(x')$ satisfies $D_{x'}v = 0$, that is $dv/d\tau = -\Omega(x') \cdot v$, with $Q(v) = 1$ ($Q(v) = 0$).
\item[(iv)] \emph{Curvature.} The curvature of $g$ is the covariant field strength: the curvature operator on physical bivectors is $B \mapsto \mathcal{R}(B)$ (in components: on the frame planes $\mathcal{R}(g_\mu \wedge g_\nu) = -R(e_\mu \wedge e_\nu)$, since $\hb(g_\mu \wedge g_\nu) = e_\mu \wedge e_\nu$, and contracted with the reciprocal planes it gives the Riemann tensor $R_{\mu\nu}{}^{\rho\sigma}$ of $g$ in the store's sign, the cited sources' $R(\hb(B))$ giving it in theirs; Fact \claimref{singularity.imported-equivalence-einstein-equations}). The Ricci map is $\mathcal{R}(b) = \partial_a \cdot \mathcal{R}(a \wedge b)$ (in components $R_{\mu\nu} = g_\mu \cdot \mathcal{R}(g_\nu)$), the scalar curvature is $\mathcal{R} = \partial_a \cdot \mathcal{R}(a)$, and the Einstein map is $\mathcal{G}(a) = \mathcal{R}(a) - \tfrac12 a\,\mathcal{R}$; the GTG field equations are Einstein's equations for $g$ (Facts \claimref{singularity.imported-equivalence-einstein-equations} and \claimref{interior.imported-equivalence-einstein-equations}). In the store's sign of the definition, $\mathcal{R}(B) = -R(\hb(B))$, the Ricci curvature of the round-sphere-positive convention on a physical null vector $k$ is $-k \cdot \mathcal{R}(k)$, and de Sitter space has $\mathcal{R}(B) = \tfrac{\Lambda}{3}B$; the cited sources use $R(\hb(B))$.
\item[(v)] \emph{Weyl and Schouten.} The Schouten tensor is $\Sch(a) = \tfrac12\bigl(\mathcal{R}(a) - \tfrac16 a\,\mathcal{R}\bigr)$, and the Weyl tensor is the trace-free part of the curvature,
\[
\mathcal{W}(a \wedge b) \;=\; \mathcal{R}(a \wedge b) - \Sch(a) \wedge b - a \wedge \Sch(b) \;=\; \mathcal{R}(a \wedge b) - \tfrac12\bigl(\mathcal{R}(a) \wedge b + a \wedge \mathcal{R}(b)\bigr) + \tfrac16\,\mathcal{R}\; a \wedge b ,
\]
with $\partial_a \cdot \mathcal{W}(a \wedge b) = 0$ and $\mathcal{W}(IB) = I\,\mathcal{W}(B)$, $I$ the pseudoscalar.
\item[(vi)] \emph{Killing vectors and surface gravity.} A vector field $\xi = \xi^\mu \partial_\mu$ is a Killing field of $g$ exactly when the physical vector field $K = \xi^\mu g_\mu = \hb^{-1}(\xi^\mu e_\mu)$ makes $A \mapsto A \cdot D K$ antisymmetric for the flat product, $B \cdot (A \cdot D K) + A \cdot (B \cdot D K) = 0$; then $A \cdot D K = A \cdot F_K$ with the bivector $F_K = \tfrac12 D \wedge K$. On a Killing horizon, a locus where $Q(K) = 0$ and $K$ is normal, the surface gravity $\kappa$ is defined by $(K \cdot D)K = \kappa K$.
\end{enumerate}
\emph{Provenance:} Lasenby, Doran and Gull \cite{LDG1998} (Sections 3.5, 4.3, 4.4, 5.1, 5.2 and Appendix C, the translation of tensor calculus), in the series' notation; \cite[Sections 13.5, 13.6, 14.1]{DoranLasenby2003}; the Weyl formula as in \cite[eq.~(8.5)]{Lasenby2019}; the surface gravity as defined in \cite[Section 12.5]{Wald1984}.
synthesis.imported-gtg-dictionary.technical:
On the region where the position-gauge field $\hb$ is invertible, every notion of the curved-spacetime description has a counterpart in Gauge Theory Gravity on flat spacetime. Tangent vectors are the physical vectors $\hb^{-1}(a)$, and a background direction is null for the derived metric exactly when $Q(\hb^{-1}(a)) = 0$. The Levi-Civita derivative is the covariant derivative $D_a = a \cdot \nabla + \Omega(a)\times$ read in the frame $g_\mu = \hb^{-1}(e_\mu)$, parallel transport is a rotor, and a geodesic is a worldline whose velocity $\hb^{-1}(x')$ is $D$-parallel.

The Riemann tensor is the covariant field strength $\mathcal{R}(B)$; the Ricci tensor, scalar curvature and Einstein tensor are its contractions, and the field equations of the two descriptions agree (the imported equivalence Facts). The Schouten tensor is $\tfrac12(\mathcal{R}(a) - a\mathcal{R}/6)$ and the Weyl tensor is the trace-free part $\mathcal{W}$ of $\mathcal{R}$, linear over the pseudoscalar. A Killing field is a physical vector field whose covariant derivative is antisymmetric, and the surface gravity of a Killing horizon is defined by $(K \cdot D)K = \kappa K$. The table is imported from the gauge-theory-gravity literature, in the series' notation.
synthesis.imported-gtg-dictionary.lay: General relativity is usually written in the language of curved spacetime: metrics, geodesics, curvature tensors. Gauge Theory Gravity writes the same physics on a flat background, with gravity carried by two fields. This imported dictionary says how each geometric notion reads in the gauge-field language: which directions light can travel in, what it means to carry a direction along a path without turning it, what a free-fall path is, and which combinations of the field strength are the familiar curvature tensors. With it, any statement made in one language can be restated in the other.

synthesis.imported-holonomy-reductions-o.formal:
Let $(\mathcal{G} \to M, \omega)$ be a Cartan geometry of type $(G, P)$ on a connected manifold $M$ (a Cartan connection, so its soldering part is nondegenerate; it need not be normal), and $\mathcal{O}$ a homogeneous space of $G$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] \emph{(Holonomy reductions.)} A holonomy reduction of $G$-type $\mathcal{O}$ is a parallel section of $\mathcal{G} \times_{P} \mathcal{O}$. For a representation $\mathbb{V}$ of $G$ with tractor bundle $\mathcal{G} \times_{P} \mathbb{V}$ and its tractor connection, a parallel section has values in a single $G$-orbit $\mathcal{O} \subset \mathbb{V}$, and is a holonomy reduction of $G$-type $\mathcal{O}$; choosing a point of $\mathcal{O}$ with isotropy group $H$, $\mathcal{O} = G/H$.
\item[(b)] \emph{(Curved orbit decomposition.)} Given a holonomy reduction of $G$-type $\mathcal{O} = G/H$, $M$ is the disjoint union of curved orbits $M_{i}$, one for each $P$-type, that is each $P$-orbit in $\mathcal{O}$ met by the section (on the homogeneous model $G/P$ these are the $H$-orbits); each $M_{i}$ is an initial submanifold and carries a canonical Cartan geometry modelled on the corresponding $H$-orbit of the model, torsion-free if $\omega$ is.
\item[(c)] \emph{(The conformal case.)} For a normal conformal Cartan connection (the normal tractor connection of a conformal structure of signature $(p, q)$) and a parallel section $s$ of the standard tractor bundle with nonzero norm, $M = M_{+} \cup M_{0} \cup M_{-}$ with $M_{0}$ the zero locus of the scale $\sigma$ of $s$, a hypersurface curved orbit with an induced conformal structure of signature $(p - 1, q)$ or $(p, q - 1)$, and on the open curved orbits $M_{\pm}$ the metric $\sigma^{-2}g$ of the conformal class is Einstein, with the sign of its Einstein constant fixed by the norm of $s$.
\end{enumerate}
\emph{Provenance:} \cite{CapGoverHammerl2014}, Definition 2.2, Lemma 2.3 and Section 2.3 for (a), Theorem 2.6 for (b), Theorem 3.5 for (c).

\emph{Reading in the series' chart (not part of the import).} With $G$ the group of $\Cl(2,4)$ rotors acting on the vectors of $\Cl(2,4)$ (the standard tractors), $P$ the stabiliser of the line of the canonical tractor $X = \nO$ and $\omega$ a $\Cl(2,4)$ gauge field on flat spacetime with nondegenerate soldering $a \mapsto A(a) \times X$, a tractor $I$ parallel for $A$ has constant $Q(I) = 2\rho$ and is, by (a), a holonomy reduction of $G$-type the level set $Q = 2\rho$, with $H$ the stabiliser of $I$ (of de Sitter type for $\rho > 0$, anti-de Sitter type for $\rho < 0$ and Poincar\'e type for $\rho = 0$). Where $\ip{X}{I} \neq 0$ the points lie on one open curved orbit, and a rotor fixing $I$ and the line of $X$ fixes $X$ (the pairing $\ip{X}{I}$ is preserved), so the induced geometry there is modelled on the stabiliser of $I$ with structure group the stabiliser of $I$ and $X$, the Lorentz group of the complement of the plane of $X$ and $I$. Clause (c) concerns the normal connection, for which a parallel scale tractor is the Einstein condition (Theorem \claimref{interior.scale-tractor-leaves-cone}); (a) and (b) do not assume normality.
synthesis.imported-holonomy-reductions-o.technical:
Cap, Gover and Hammerl develop holonomy reductions for general Cartan geometries. A Cartan geometry of type $(G, P)$ is a manifold modelled on the homogeneous space $G/P$ by a Cartan connection; a parallel section of an associated bundle whose fibre is a homogeneous space of $G$ is a holonomy reduction. For a tractor bundle (associated with a representation of $G$), a parallel section takes values in one $G$-orbit, so it is a holonomy reduction of that orbit type, with structure group reduced to the isotropy group $H$ of a point. Given such a reduction the manifold splits into curved orbits, one for each $P$-orbit in the $G$-orbit, which are initial submanifolds, each carrying an induced Cartan geometry modelled on the matching $H$-orbit of $G/P$, torsion-free when the original is. None of this assumes the Cartan connection is normal. In conformal geometry, with the normal tractor connection and a parallel standard tractor of nonzero norm, the zero set of its scale is a hypersurface separating two open curved orbits, on which the rescaled metric $\sigma^{-2}g$ is Einstein.

In the series' chart the standard tractors are the vectors of $\Cl(2,4)$, $P$ is the stabiliser of the line of the canonical tractor $X$, and a parallel tractor $I$ of norm $2\rho$ reduces a $\Cl(2,4)$ gauge field with nondegenerate soldering to the stabiliser of $I$ (de Sitter, anti-de Sitter or Poincar\'e type); where $\ip{X}{I} \neq 0$ the induced geometry has the Lorentz group as structure group. For the normal connection the parallel scale tractor is the Einstein condition; for a connection that is not required to be normal it is a reduction of the field.
synthesis.imported-holonomy-reductions-o.lay: A Cartan geometry describes a curved space by comparing it, point by point, with a simple symmetric model space. Cap, Gover and Hammerl showed that whenever such a geometry carries a quantity that stays fixed as it is transported around, the space breaks into pieces, each with its own simpler geometry of the same kind, and that this works whether or not the geometry obeys the usual normalisation. For the conformal geometry of spacetime with its standard normalisation, if a fixed quantity of this kind has nonzero length, it singles out a metric solving Einstein's equations on the parts where its scale is nonzero. This is a result taken from the mathematical literature.

imported_from.citation: A. Cap, A. R. Gover and M. Hammerl, Holonomy reductions of Cartan geometries and curved orbit decompositions, Duke Math. J. 163 (2014), 1035--1070.
imported_from.locator: Definition 2.2, Lemma 2.3 and Section 2.3, Theorem 2.6, Theorem 3.5 (arXiv:1103.4497)

synthesis.imported-ikeda-taniguchi-spect.formal: On the round unit sphere $S^{n}$, $n \ge 2$, the Hodge Laplacian $\Delta = d\delta + \delta d$ on functions has eigenvalues $l(l + n - 1)$, $l \ge 0$, with multiplicity $\binom{n + l}{n} - \binom{n + l - 2}{n}$ (the harmonic polynomials of degree $l$). On one-forms every nonzero eigenspace splits into exact and coexact parts, which $d$ and $\delta$ exchange: the exact forms $d\phi$ carry the nonzero eigenvalues of functions, and the coexact forms carry the eigenvalues $(l + 1)(l + n - 2)$, $l \ge 1$, each on one irreducible $SO(n + 1)$-module. In particular the coexact eigenvalues are $(l + 1)^{2}$ with multiplicity $2l(l + 2)$ on $S^{3}$, and $(l + 1)(l + 2)$ with multiplicity $\tfrac12 l(l + 3)(2l + 3)$ on $S^{4}$, $l \ge 1$ \cite{IkedaTaniguchi1978}. The spheres here are closed Riemannian manifolds, not gravitational fields on flat spacetime; the store uses these spectra only through the local heat-kernel densities they reproduce, as a Euclidean reading.
synthesis.imported-ikeda-taniguchi-spect.technical: The Laplacian on the round sphere is diagonalised by the representation theory of its rotation group: each eigenspace is an irreducible module, and its eigenvalue is a Casimir value. For one-forms the gradients of the scalar harmonics carry the scalar eigenvalues, and the divergence-free (coexact) forms carry $(l + 1)(l + n - 2)$. On the three-sphere these are the photon modes of the Einstein static universe, $(l + 1)^{2}$ with $2l(l + 2)$ states, two helicities; on the four-sphere they are $(l + 1)(l + 2)$ with $\tfrac12 l(l + 3)(2l + 3)$ states, the first level being the ten Killing vectors.
synthesis.imported-ikeda-taniguchi-spect.lay: On a perfectly round sphere, waves of any kind can only vibrate at certain frequencies, fixed by the sphere's symmetry. Ikeda and Taniguchi listed these frequencies for the various kinds of waves, including the ones that describe light. The series uses their list when it counts how the light-like fields contribute to the strength of gravity induced by quantum fluctuations.

imported_from.citation: A. Ikeda and Y. Taniguchi, Spectra and eigenforms of the Laplacian on $S^{n}$ and $P^{n}(\mathbb{C})$, Osaka J. Math. 15 (1978), no. 3, 515--546.
imported_from.locator: Sec. 1 (decomposition of eigenforms into closed and coclosed parts); Thm. 4.2 (eigenvalues on the irreducible submodules of p-forms on S^n)

synthesis.imported-jacobson-clausius-199.technical: Jacobson derived Einstein's equation from thermodynamics; in Gauge Theory Gravity it is the field equation of the gravitational field $(\hb, \Omega)$ on flat spacetime. Through every point and in every physically null direction, consider a small local Rindler horizon whose generators are momentarily neither expanding nor shearing. Assume that it has the Unruh temperature of the accelerated observers just inside it, that its entropy is a universal constant $\eta$ times its area, and that the heat crossing it, the boost energy of matter, obeys $\delta Q = T\,\delta S$. The Raychaudhuri equation turns the area change into the Ricci map of the field strength along the null direction, so the Clausius relation for all null directions gives $T_{ab}k^{a}k^{b} = (\eta/2\pi)R_{ab}k^{a}k^{b}$, that is $k \cdot T(k) = -(\eta/2\pi)\,k \cdot \mathcal{R}(k)$ in the store's sign. Energy conservation and the Bianchi identity then give Einstein's equation, $\mathcal{G}(a) + \Lambda a = -(2\pi/\eta)T(a)$, with Newton's constant $1/(4\eta)$ and a cosmological constant left undetermined as an integration constant.
synthesis.imported-jacobson-clausius-199.lay: In 1995 Ted Jacobson showed that Einstein's equations can be read as a law of thermodynamics. If every small patch of horizon, as seen by an accelerating observer, has a temperature set by the acceleration and an entropy proportional to its area, and if heat crossing it changes its entropy by heat divided by temperature, then the gravitational field must obey exactly Einstein's equations, read here as the equations of a field on flat spacetime. The strength of gravity is fixed by the entropy per area, and the cosmological constant is left free. This is a known result taken from the literature.

imported_from.citation: T. Jacobson, Thermodynamics of spacetime: the Einstein equation of state, Phys. Rev. Lett. 75 (1995), 1260--1263.

synthesis.imported-jacobson-entanglement.formal:
Units $\hbar = c = 1$, spacetime dimension $d$, signature $(-,+,\ldots,+)$ with the round sphere of positive scalar curvature. Spacetime is a gravitational field $(\hb, \Omega)$ on flat $\R^{d-1,1}$, with the product of the declared signature (the $d$-dimensional clause of Definition \claimref{obj.synthesis.gtg-flat-spacetime-gauge-fields}), and the geometric quantities below are those of its derived metric, read through Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-gtg-dictionary}. About any point and for any unit timelike vector $u$, let $B$ be a small geodesic ball of radius $\ell$ in the slice orthogonal to $u$ (in Gauge Theory Gravity: the geodesic ball of the derived metric, described in a gauge with $\hb(x_0) = 1$, $\Omega(x_0) = 0$ about a point $x_0$ of the background, the frame transported along straight background rays), compared with a maximally symmetric reference geometry and the vacuum of the quantum fields. Suppose (a) the ultraviolet entanglement across $\partial B$ has a finite universal area density $\eta$; (b) the fields are conformal, so that the modular Hamiltonian of the vacuum on the causal diamond of $B$ is $2\pi$ times the generator $H_{\zeta}$ of its conformal Killing flow, whence for first-order variations $\delta S_{\mathrm{matter}} = 2\pi\,\delta\langle H_{\zeta}\rangle = 2\pi\,\Omega_{d-2}\ell^{d}\,\delta\langle T_{00}\rangle/(d^{2} - 1)$ to leading order in $\ell$; while geometrically, at fixed volume, $\delta A|_{V} = -\Omega_{d-2}\ell^{d}\,G_{00}/(d^{2} - 1)$. Then the total entanglement $\eta\,\delta A|_{V} + \delta S_{\mathrm{matter}}$ is stationary for every such ball, at every point and for every $u$, if and only if
\[
G_{ab} + \Lambda g_{ab} \;=\; \frac{2\pi}{\eta}\,\delta\langle T_{ab}\rangle ,
\]
with $\Lambda$ a constant fixed by no part of the argument (it enters as an integration constant through the contracted Bianchi identity and conservation): Einstein's equation with $G = 1/(4\eta)$. The passage from the $00$ component for every $u$ at every point to the tensor equation is part of the argument. For nonconformal fields the same conclusion holds modulo a stated conjecture on $\delta\langle K\rangle$. \emph{Provenance:} \cite{Jacobson2016}.
synthesis.imported-jacobson-entanglement.technical: Jacobson's maximal vacuum entanglement hypothesis says that the entanglement entropy of a small geodesic ball is maximal, at fixed volume, in a locally maximally symmetric vacuum of geometry and quantum fields. In Gauge Theory Gravity, in any dimension $d$, the ball is taken about a point of the flat background in the normal gauge of the gravitational field. Varying the gravitational and matter fields together to first order, the area term changes by $\eta\,\delta A|_{V} = -\eta\,\Omega_{d-2}\ell^{d}G_{00}/(d^{2} - 1)$ and, for conformal fields, the matter term by $2\pi\,\Omega_{d-2}\ell^{d}\,\delta\langle T_{00}\rangle/(d^{2} - 1)$, using the conformal Killing modular Hamiltonian of the ball's causal diamond. Stationarity for all balls, at all points and in all frames, holds exactly when $G_{ab} + \Lambda g_{ab} = (2\pi/\eta)\,\delta\langle T_{ab}\rangle$, with $\Lambda$ an integration constant: Einstein's equation with $G = 1/(4\eta)$. Nonconformal fields need an additional conjecture.
synthesis.imported-jacobson-entanglement.lay: In 2016 Ted Jacobson showed that Einstein's equations follow if empty space is as entangled as it can be. Take any small ball of space; the quantum fields inside are entangled with those outside, by an amount proportional to the ball's surface area, plus a contribution from any matter present. Requiring that this total entanglement is at a maximum, for every small ball at every place and as seen by every observer, turns out to be the same as requiring Einstein's equations. This is a known result taken from the literature.

imported_from.citation: T. Jacobson, Entanglement equilibrium and the Einstein equation, Phys. Rev. Lett. 116 (2016), 201101.

synthesis.imported-lovelock-and-anderson.technical: Lovelock's theorem is the classical uniqueness result for Einstein's equations: in four dimensions, any field equation for the metric that is built covariantly from the metric and its first two derivatives and is automatically divergence-free (as the field equations of a covariant action are, by Noether's second theorem) is a combination of the Einstein tensor and the metric. Field equations of an action of second order are therefore Einstein's, with one value of the cosmological constant. Anderson and Duchamp developed the inverse problem of the calculus of variations (when a given differential equation is the Euler-Lagrange equation of some action), and Anderson treated actions invariant under the symmetries of the metric. The part used here is that the covariant actions of a four-dimensional metric with no field equations at all are the Euler (Gauss-Bonnet) and Pontryagin densities plus total divergences, so two covariant actions with the same field equations differ only by those. Taken from the literature; in Gauge Theory Gravity the metric is the derived metric of the gravitational field on flat spacetime.
synthesis.imported-lovelock-and-anderson.lay: Einstein's equations are not just one choice among many. Lovelock proved that in a four-dimensional world, if the equations for gravity involve the geometry and its rates of change no more than twice over, and automatically respect energy conservation, they must be Einstein's equations with some cosmological constant. Anderson and Duchamp studied the reverse question, when a set of equations comes from an action principle, and the part used here says that two such principles giving the same equations can differ only by terms that measure the overall shape of space. These are theorems taken from the literature.

imported_from.citation: D. Lovelock, The Einstein tensor and its generalizations, J. Math. Phys. 12 (1971), 498--501.
D. Lovelock, The four-dimensionality of space and the Einstein tensor, J. Math. Phys. 13 (1972), 874--876.
I. M. Anderson and T. Duchamp, On the existence of global variational principles, Amer. J. Math. 102 (1980), 781--868.
I. M. Anderson, Natural variational principles on Riemannian structures, Ann. of Math. (2) 120 (1984), 329--370.

synthesis.imported-lovelock-cartan-four-.formal:
Let $(\hb, \Omega)$ be a gravitational field on four-dimensional flat spacetime (Definition \claimref{obj.synthesis.gtg-flat-spacetime-gauge-fields}), with the frame and the rotation gauge field varied independently (first-order variables). Write $e(a) = \hb^{-1}(a)$ for the soldering form (a vector-valued one-form), $R$ for the field strength of $\Omega$ written as a bivector-valued two-form, and $T = De$ for the torsion (a vector-valued two-form); $I_{4}$ is the spacetime pseudoscalar.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] (Mardones and Zanelli.) The four-forms invariant under local rotations that are polynomial in $e$, $R$ and $T$, built with the exterior product of forms and the geometric product of their values, with no Hodge dual and no inverse frame, are, up to exact forms, combinations of: the scalar and $I_{4}$ parts of $R \wedge R$ (the Pontryagin density and the Euler density), of $(e \wedge e) \wedge R$ (the Holst-type density and the Einstein-Hilbert density), and of $(e \wedge e) \wedge (e \wedge e)$ (the $I_{4}$ part is the volume), and the torsion square, the scalar part of $T \wedge T$ with the vector values multiplied by the inner product (index readings: $R^{ab}R_{ab}$, $\epsilon_{abcd}R^{ab}R^{cd}$, $e^{a}e^{b}R_{ab}$, $\epsilon_{abcd}R^{ab}e^{c}e^{d}$, $\epsilon_{abcd}e^{a}e^{b}e^{c}e^{d}$, $T^{a}T_{a}$). The Pontryagin density and the Nieh-Yan combination $T^{a}T_{a} - e^{a}e^{b}R_{ab}$ are exact; the Euler density is locally exact. In $n$ dimensions the same construction gives the Lovelock series together with a finite list of torsional terms.
\item[(b)] (Holst.) Adding to the Einstein-Cartan (Palatini) functional with cosmological term the Holst term, a constant multiple $1/\gamma$ ($\gamma$ real and nonzero) of the Holst-type density $e^{a} \wedge e^{b} \wedge R_{ab}$, leaves the vacuum field equations unchanged: without matter the connection equation still forces zero torsion, and on torsion-free fields the Holst density's contribution to the frame equation vanishes by the cyclic (first Bianchi) identity of the curvature. The canonical analysis of the modified functional gives Barbero's real connection variables, with $\gamma$ the Barbero-Immirzi parameter.
\end{enumerate}
\emph{Note (the Barbero-Immirzi contact term; readings from the literature).} With spinning matter the torsion is fixed algebraically by the spin density (Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-einstein-cartan-matter-coupling}), and the Holst term no longer drops out: with minimally coupled fermions $\gamma$ sets the strength of the resulting four-fermion contact interaction \cite{PerezRovelli2006}; with minimal coupling parity is preserved, and a non-minimal coupling of the fermions to torsion violates it \cite{FreidelMinicTakeuchi2005}.

\emph{Provenance:} \cite{MardonesZanelli1991} for (a), with the four-dimensional list as in \cite{Zanelli2005}; \cite{Holst1996} for (b).
synthesis.imported-lovelock-cartan-four-.technical: When gravity is written with the frame and the rotation gauge field as independent fields, the possible actions in four dimensions that use only exterior products (no Hodge dual, no inverse frame) form a short list, worked out in general by Mardones and Zanelli: the Euler (Gauss-Bonnet), Einstein-Hilbert and volume terms, the Pontryagin density, the term pairing the frame square with the curvature without the alternating symbol (the Holst-type term), and the torsion square; the Pontryagin and Nieh-Yan combinations are total derivatives. Holst showed that adding the Holst-type term with coefficient $1/\gamma$ to the usual first-order action does not change the vacuum field equations, because it is inert on torsion-free fields, and that its Hamiltonian form gives Barbero's real connection variables with the Barbero-Immirzi parameter $\gamma$. As a note: with spinning matter the torsion is not zero, and the literature finds that the term then sets the strength of a four-fermion contact interaction (Perez and Rovelli), and that parity is kept for minimal coupling and broken by non-minimal coupling to torsion (Freidel, Minic and Takeuchi). Taken from the literature.
synthesis.imported-lovelock-cartan-four-.lay: If gravity is described like the other forces, with two independent ingredients, only a handful of building blocks for its law are possible in four dimensions; Mardones and Zanelli listed them. One of them, studied by Holst, has no effect at all on gravity in empty space, which is why it is free to be added; it matters only when matter with spin is present, where it changes a very weak spin-spin force. These results are taken from the literature.

synthesis.imported-nordstrom-scalar-theo.formal:
Let $(\hb, \Omega)$ be a torsion-free gravitational field on four-dimensional flat spacetime, signature $(+,-,-,-)$ (Definition \claimref{obj.synthesis.gtg-flat-spacetime-gauge-fields}), with store curvature $\mathcal{R}$ and Weyl curvature $\mathcal{W}$, its scalar curvature also written $\mathcal{R}$ in the store's sign (as in Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-gtg-dictionary}), coupled to matter with a symmetric stress map $T$ of trace $\tau$ ($\tau = \rho$ for dust), conserved by the matter's own equations. \emph{Nordstr\"om's theory in the form of Einstein and Fokker} is the pair of field equations
\[
\mathcal{W} = 0, \qquad \mathcal{R} = -24\pi G\,\tau,
\]
that is, in the signature $(-,+,+,+)$ and round-sphere-positive curvature of the sources, $C_{abcd} = 0$ and $R = 24\pi G\,T$ with $T = -\rho$ for dust: the derived metric is conformally flat and its scalar curvature is sourced by the trace of the stress alone. Its observational consequences: (a) light (any massless particle) moves on null geodesics, which are invariant under conformal rescaling, so it is not deflected (post-Newtonian parameter $\gamma = -1$, where Einstein's equations give $\gamma = 1$); (b) the perihelion advance of a planetary orbit is $-\tfrac16$ of the value Einstein's equations give ($\beta = \tfrac12$). Since light deflection and the perihelion advance agree with Einstein's values, the theory is excluded by observation. \emph{Provenance:} \cite{EinsteinFokker1914}, the scalar theory \cite{Nordstrom1913}; the field equations and both failures in modern form \cite[Sec.~II.3, Eq.~(3.7)]{DeruelleSasaki2011}; \cite[Exercise~7.1]{MTW1973}.
synthesis.imported-nordstrom-scalar-theo.technical: Nordstr\"om's 1913 theory was the most developed relativistic theory of gravity before general relativity: gravity is one scalar field sourced by the trace of the matter's stress-energy. Einstein and Fokker showed in 1914 that it is a geometric theory: the spacetime metric is conformally flat (the Weyl curvature vanishes) and its scalar curvature is proportional to the stress trace, with matter moving on geodesics. In the store's language the field equations are $\mathcal{W} = 0$ and $\mathcal{R} = -24\pi G\tau$. The theory is consistent and has the Newtonian limit, but it fails two classical tests: because null geodesics do not change under a conformal rescaling of the metric, it predicts no bending of light, and it predicts a perihelion advance of minus one sixth of general relativity's, a retrograde shift. Both are contradicted by observation.
synthesis.imported-nordstrom-scalar-theo.lay: Before Einstein completed general relativity, Nordstr\"om proposed a simpler theory in which gravity is a single number at each point, produced by the total energy content of matter. Einstein and Fokker showed it can be written as geometry. It reproduces Newton's law, but it predicts that light is not bent by the Sun and that Mercury's orbit turns slightly backwards rather than forwards, both of which observation rules out. These are taken from the literature.

synthesis.imported-raychaudhuri-null-con.formal:
Let $(\hb, \Omega)$ be a gravitational field on flat spacetime with covariant derivative $D$ (Definition \claimref{obj.synthesis.gtg-flat-spacetime-gauge-fields}) whose derived metric is $C^{2}$, and let $k$ be a physical null vector field ($Q(k) = 0$) tangent to an affinely parametrised congruence of null geodesics, $(k \cdot D)\,k = 0$, with parameter $\lambda$, so that $d/d\lambda = k \cdot D$ (components $k^{a}$). Let $\theta$, $\sigma_{ab}$ and $\omega_{ab}$ be its expansion, shear and twist: the trace, symmetric trace-free part and antisymmetric part of the map $A \mapsto A \cdot D k$ on a two-dimensional screen space of physical vectors orthogonal to $k$. Write $\Ric^{\circ}$ for the Ricci tensor of the convention in which the round sphere has positive Ricci curvature, so that $\Ric^{\circ}(k,k) = -k \cdot \mathcal{R}(k)$ with the store's curvature operator, and $C$ for the Weyl tensor of that convention, read from the Weyl map $\mathcal{W}$ of the field strength. Then
\[
\frac{d\theta}{d\lambda} = -\tfrac12\,\theta^{2} - \sigma_{ab}\sigma^{ab} + \omega_{ab}\omega^{ab} - \Ric^{\circ}_{ab}k^{a}k^{b},
\qquad
\frac{d\sigma_{ab}}{d\lambda} = -\theta\,\sigma_{ab} - \widehat{C_{cadb}k^{c}k^{d}},
\]
the hat denoting the trace-free projection onto the screen space; the twist vanishes for the generators of a null hypersurface. In the store's sign the focusing equation reads $(k \cdot D)\,\theta = -\tfrac12\theta^{2} - \sigma_{ab}\sigma^{ab} + \omega_{ab}\omega^{ab} + k \cdot \mathcal{R}(k)$, and in signature $(+,-,-,-)$ the shear source $C_{cadb}k^{c}k^{d}$ is the form $(a, b) \mapsto (k \wedge b) \cdot \mathcal{W}(k \wedge a)$ on the screen space. \emph{Provenance:} \cite{Raychaudhuri1955} (the focusing equation, timelike case), \cite{Sachs1961} (the optical scalars and the null equations), \cite{Wald1984} (Section 9.2).
synthesis.imported-raychaudhuri-null-con.technical: These are the standard propagation equations for a bundle of light rays; in Gauge Theory Gravity they are written for a field of physical null vectors on flat spacetime, with the covariant derivative along the rays. The expansion measures how fast the cross-sectional area of the bundle grows, the shear how it is distorted, the twist how it rotates. Along the rays the expansion decreases by half its square, by the squared shear and by the Ricci curvature along the ray (the term $-k \cdot \mathcal{R}(k)$ of the field strength in the store's sign), and increases with the twist, which is zero for the generators of a null hypersurface such as a horizon. The shear is sourced by the Weyl part of the field strength along the ray and damped by the expansion. In a horizon patch whose expansion and shear vanish at a point, the area change to leading order is set by the Ricci term alone, which is how Jacobson's argument turns heat flux into curvature.
synthesis.imported-raychaudhuri-null-con.lay: Light rays travelling side by side can converge or spread out. Raychaudhuri and Sachs found the equations that say how a bundle of rays changes as it travels: matter and the gravitational field along the rays focus them together, and a separate part of the field strength squeezes the bundle out of shape. These equations are standard textbook geometry; the series uses them in the step where the energy flowing through a small horizon is converted into the strength of the gravitational field.

synthesis.imported-sakharov-induced-grav.formal:
Work in Euclidean signature with scalar curvature $R$ positive on spheres (the sources' convention).
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(a)] (Vassilevich, the curvature-linear heat-kernel coefficient.) For a Laplace-type operator $D = -(g^{\mu\nu}\nabla_{\mu}\nabla_{\nu} + E)$ on a vector bundle $V$ over a closed $n$-dimensional Riemannian manifold, the heat trace $\mathrm{Tr}(f e^{-tD})$ has the coefficient linear in curvature $a_{2}(f, D) = (4\pi)^{-n/2}\tfrac16\int_{M}\mathrm{tr}_{V}\big(f(6E + R)\big)$: the local density is $\mathrm{tr}_{V}(E + R/6)$ (the store's proofs write it $a_{1}$, the coefficient of the first power of the heat-kernel time). For a scalar coupled to the curvature with strength $\xi$, $E = -\xi R$ and the density is $(1 - 6\xi)R/6$.
\item[(b)] (Broda and Szanecki, Sakharov's induced gravity.) At one loop with an ultraviolet cut-off $\epsilon$, the matter fields induce the Einstein-Hilbert term $-\tfrac{1}{192\pi^{2}\epsilon}(N_{0} + N_{1/2} - 4N_{1})R$, with $N_{0}$ the number of minimally coupled scalars, $N_{1/2}$ the number of two-component fermion fields and $N_{1}$ the number of gauge vectors; with (a), a scalar of coupling $\xi$ contributes $N_{0}(1 - 6\xi)$ in place of $N_{0}$.
\item[(c)] (Boyle and Turok.) Cancelling the vacuum energy and both coefficients of the Weyl anomaly of the Standard Model by conformally coupled dimension-zero scalars requires $n_{1/2} = 4n_{1}$ Weyl fermions (with $n'_{0} = 3n_{1}$, $n_{0} = 0$); with the twelve gauge vectors of the Standard Model, $n_{1/2} = 48 = 3 \times 16$, three generations including right-handed neutrinos.
\item[(d)] (Tichy and Flanagan.) For a massless field the renormalised stress tensor is fixed by Wald's axioms up to $\alpha H^{(1)}_{ab} + \beta H^{(2)}_{ab}$, the two conserved local curvature tensors of dimension $(\mathrm{mass})^{4}$; no Einstein-tensor term and no metric term is allowed, since either would need a dimensionful coefficient.
\end{enumerate}
\emph{Provenance:} \cite[Eq.~(4.27)]{Vassilevich2003}; \cite[Eqs.~(5), (8)]{BrodaSzanecki2009}; \cite[Eq.~(17)]{BoyleTurok2021}; \cite[Sec.~I.A]{TichyFlanagan1998}.
synthesis.imported-sakharov-induced-grav.technical: Sakharov proposed that Newton's constant is induced by the vacuum fluctuations of the matter and gauge fields. At one loop the induced coefficient of the scalar curvature in the effective action comes from the heat-kernel coefficient linear in curvature, whose density for an operator $-(\nabla^{2} + E)$ is the trace of $E + R/6$. Summing over species with a cut-off gives a coefficient proportional to $N_{0} + N_{1/2} - 4N_{1}$, counting minimally coupled scalars, two-component fermions and gauge vectors; a scalar coupled to curvature with strength $\xi$ counts with weight $1 - 6\xi$, zero for conformal coupling. Boyle and Turok, cancelling the vacuum energy and the Weyl anomaly by a different mechanism, arrive at the same count of four Weyl fermions per gauge vector, which the Standard Model with twelve gauge vectors meets at exactly three generations including right-handed neutrinos. In the locally covariant scheme of Wald's axioms, by contrast, the stress tensor of a massless field has no Einstein-tensor ambiguity at all, whatever the field content.
synthesis.imported-sakharov-induced-grav.lay: One idea for where the strength of gravity comes from is that it is induced by the quantum jitter of all the particle fields, like the stiffness of a material coming from its atoms. In the simplest version each kind of field contributes a fixed weight, and force-carrying fields count four times as strongly, with the opposite sign, as matter fields. With the known particles plus right-handed neutrinos, the matter fields number exactly four times the force carriers, a coincidence noticed in another context by Boyle and Turok. These are taken from the literature.

synthesis.infinity-vacuum-incidence-is-a.technical: The stored theorem reads Einstein's condition as the infinity vacua, the Fock vacua annihilated by the pure-scale tractor, being unexcited along their own null rays, which point vacua are in every metric. The open question was why infinity should obey what every point obeys. Three results answer it as far as the store's objects allow. First, transport: along a null geodesic, the span of the canonical tractor and the ray's tractor is parallel in every metric, so a point vacuum carried along its own ray stays a point vacuum to all orders; the pure-scale tractor and the ray's tractor span a parallel plane exactly when the metric is Einstein, so then infinity vacua do the same. Second, blindness, an elementary observation (the Einstein condition is not conformally invariant): everything the store places on the CAR side (the Fock module with its anticommutation relations, the tractor connection, the canonical tractor and the point vacua) depends only on the conformal class, while the infinity vacua's classes depend on the second derivatives of the scale. The flat metric and its rescaling by $1 + a x_{1}^{2}$ agree at the origin in all of those data and in the infinity vacua themselves, yet one is Einstein there and the other is not. No condition on the conformal CAR data can force the incidence; a reason must select the scale. Third, the selection that works, which is the known almost-Einstein characterisation restated: the pure-scale tractor is the null projection, along the canonical tractor, of $I' = I_{g} + (J/4)X$, by the same formula that embeds points as null vectors, and the infinity vacua's own-ray classes are those of $I'$. They vanish exactly when $I'$ is parallel, that is when the scale is the scale of a frozen point, and then the cosmological constant is the frozen point's integration constant. With matter, the standard formula for the scale tractor's derivative with Einstein's equations substituted says that the scale tractor's covariant derivative is $4\pi G$ times the trace-free stress tensor, with the trace's gradient in the last slot; this rewrites the field equations and is a law only for a stress tensor given independently of the vacuum field. The parts (3) and (4) are the almost-Einstein characterisation of conformal geometry read through the vacua; (1) and (2) are new in the store, (2) being elementary. The missing piece is now precise: a principle, quantum or otherwise, that selects the frozen-point scale.
synthesis.infinity-vacuum-incidence-is-a.lay: In the series, each point of spacetime carries a family of quantum vacuum states, and so does the "point at infinity" that a choice of length scale singles out. Einstein's equations are equivalent to the statement that the vacua at infinity are never disturbed when moved along their own light rays, which the vacua of ordinary points never are, in any spacetime. This result shows first that the property holds along whole light rays, not only at the start. It then shows that the question "why does infinity behave like a point?" cannot be answered from the quantum side alone: two spacetimes that look identical to every quantum structure the series attaches to points can differ in exactly this property, because it depends on the choice of length scale, which the quantum side does not see. What does answer it, by a known result of conformal geometry restated here, is a fixed object of the series, the frozen point: infinity behaves like a point exactly when it is a frozen, unchanging object plus a piece of an ordinary point. With matter present, the object that is the frozen point in empty space is no longer unchanging, and how it changes is the matter's energy and stress; this rewrites Einstein's equations rather than explaining them.

synthesis.integrated-loc-curvature-claus.formal:
Units $\hbar = c = G = 1$. Store sign (Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-gtg-dictionary}): signature $(+,-,-,-)$ on the physical vectors, $\mathcal{R}(B)$ the curvature of a gravitational field $(\hb, \Omega)$ on flat spacetime (Definition \claimref{obj.synthesis.gtg-flat-spacetime-gauge-fields}), $\mathcal{R}(b)$ its Ricci map, $\mathcal{G}(b)$ its Einstein map, de Sitter $\mathcal{R}(B) = \tfrac{\Lambda}{3}B$, field equations $\mathcal{G}(b) + \Lambda b = -8\pi G_{e}\,T(b)$, a perfect fluid at rest $T(b) = (\rho + p)(b\cdot\gamma_{0})\gamma_{0} - p\,b$. Write $t = 2\pi T$ and ${}^{\circ}$ for the trace-free part of a symmetric map. The \emph{local data} at a point $p$ are $\mathcal{R}$ and $t$ at $p$, up to proper Lorentz transformations of the physical vectors; the density is taken independent of the patch's null direction and edge plane, as in Theorem \claimref{synthesis.c-loc-entropy-clause-curvature-independent-density}(iv) (a function on the invertible region). On the integrated reading of Premise \claimref{synthesis.c-loc-local-horizon-premise} the entropy of a cut is $\int\eta\,dA$; here $\eta(p) = f(\text{local data at } p)$ for a function $f$ that is continuous and makes $\eta$ a $C^{1}$ function on each admissible field (a gravitational field with matter on a connected open part of its invertible region, derived metric $C^{3}$, satisfying hypotheses (H1) to (H4) of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.einstein-equations-from-c-loc-and-clausius} with this density). \emph{Calibrated data}: de Sitter curvature $\tfrac{\Lambda}{3}B$, $\Lambda > 0$, with $t = 0$, where the store's de Sitter entropy gives $\eta = \tfrac14$ (Theorem \claimref{synthesis.c-loc-entropy-clause-curvature-independent-density}(ii)), and their limit $\Lambda \to 0$, the flat data.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] \emph{(Asymptotic calibration.)} If an admissible field contains points whose local data converge to calibrated data, then $\eta = \tfrac14$ throughout it and its field equations hold with $G_{e} = 1$.
\item[(ii)] \emph{(Friedmann instants.)} For the flat Friedmann field $\hb^{-1}(e_{0}) = e_{0}$, $\hb^{-1}(e_{i}) = a(t)\,e_{i}$, at an instant with $a = 1$, $\dot a = a_{1}$, $\ddot a = a_{2}$: $\mathcal{R}(\gamma_{i}\wedge\gamma_{j}) = a_{1}^{2}\,\gamma_{i}\wedge\gamma_{j}$, $\mathcal{R}(\gamma_{0}\wedge\gamma_{i}) = a_{2}\,\gamma_{0}\wedge\gamma_{i}$, and the Weyl part vanishes. With a perfect fluid at rest, $s = 8\pi G_{e}\rho > 0$, $p = w\rho$, and $\Lambda$, the field equations hold at the instant if and only if $a_{1}^{2} = (s + \Lambda)/3$ and $a_{2} = -s(1 + 3w)/6 + \Lambda/3$, so $\mathcal{R}$ is $\tfrac{\Lambda}{3}B$ plus $s$ times a fixed operator. For $w \in [0, 1]$ and $\Lambda \ge 0$ the expanding field has $\rho$ decreasing continuously to $0$ as $t \to \infty$, so its local data tend to calibrated data. Every isotropic Weyl-free curvature with space-plane value $\beta > 0$ and time-plane value $\alpha$, $-2\beta \le \alpha < \beta$, is the curvature at an instant of such a field (with $w \in [0,1]$, $\Lambda \in [0, 3\beta)$).
\item[(iii)] \emph{(The curvature clause.)} Hence, if $f$ depends on the curvature only and the admissible class contains the flat Friedmann fields of (ii), each with the coupling its Clausius relation fixes, then $f = \tfrac14$ at every isotropic Weyl-free curvature with $\beta > 0$ and $-2\beta \le \alpha \le \beta$. The Einstein static universe of radius $A$, with any perfect fluid, has the curvature $\beta = 1/A^{2}$, $\alpha = 0$ of the flat dust Friedmann field with $\Lambda = 1/A^{2}$ at its inflection instant ($8\pi G_{e}\rho = 2/A^{2}$, $\ddot a = 0$). So every continuous curvature-only density, the density $\tfrac14(1 + c\,S_{ab}S^{ab})$ of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.loc-independent-of-clausius-and-killing-data} among them, is $\tfrac14$ at the Einstein static universe's curvature once those Friedmann fields are admissible; that model escapes because its admissible class (fields on which $S_{ab}S^{ab}$ is constant) omits them.
\item[(iv)] \emph{(Not the constancy of the arguments.)} Along flat dust Friedmann with $\Lambda = 0$ the scalar curvature varies while $S_{ab}S^{ab} = \tfrac34\mathcal{R}^{2}$ at every instant, so the density $\tfrac14(1 + c\,S_{ab}S^{ab}/\mathcal{R}^{2})$ is the constant $\tfrac14(1 + \tfrac34 c)$ there and (H1) holds with $G_{e} = 1/(1 + \tfrac34 c)$, on a field whose arguments vary along every null direction. That density is not defined at Ricci-flat data, so it is not continuous at the calibrated flat data; for continuous densities the confinement takes the form (i).
\item[(v)] \emph{(The matter clause is independent.)} Let $X(b) = \mathcal{R}^{\circ}(b) + 4\,t^{\circ}(b)$, $Q = \sum_{m} X(\gamma_{m})\cdot X(\gamma^{m})$ and $\eta = \tfrac14(1 + cQ)$, a polynomial in the local data. On every pair satisfying the field equations with $G_{e} = 1$ and any $\Lambda$, $X = 0$ and $\eta = \tfrac14$, so every such pair is admissible. On the Einstein static universe of radius $2$ with $\Lambda = \tfrac14$ and dust $t(b) = \tfrac14(b\cdot\gamma_{0})\gamma_{0}$, with $c = \tfrac{16}{3}$: $Q = \tfrac{3}{16}$, $\eta = \tfrac12$, the field equations hold with $G_{e} = \tfrac12$, and the leading Clausius defect $t(k,k) + \eta\,k\cdot\mathcal{R}(k)$ vanishes for every null $k$, so (H1) holds on every patch. With Clausius, calibration, continuity and every field satisfying Einstein's equations at $G_{e} = 1$ admissible, the independence of $\eta$ from matter is not derived.
\item[(vi)] \emph{(What (Loc) adds.)} On the integrated reading, beyond the Clausius relation, the calibration and continuity, (Loc) adds (a) curvature independence at curvature values that no asymptotically calibrated admissible field passes through, and (b) one coupling for admissible fields whose local data stay away from calibrated data, of which the Einstein static universe is an example.
\end{enumerate}
Beyond one flat chart: the Einstein static universe's spatial sections are closed; every statement about it is local and is made on its stereographic chart.
synthesis.integrated-loc-curvature-claus.technical:
The Clausius route derives Einstein's equations from (Loc), whose content is that the entropy per unit area of a small horizon patch is one constant. On the integrated reading the Clausius relation already forces the density to be constant along each gravitational field, and the store records that a curvature-dependent density can then fail only on fields with no calibrated vacuum point. This result sharpens that in both directions.

For a continuous density, a field whose local data come arbitrarily close to calibrated data has density $\tfrac14$, because the density is constant along it and tends to $\tfrac14$. Flat Friedmann universes with ordinary fluids and $\Lambda \ge 0$ are such fields: they dilute toward de Sitter or flat space. At each instant their curvature is isotropic and Weyl-free, and between them they pass through every such curvature with $\beta > 0$ and $-2\beta \le \alpha < \beta$. The Einstein static universe, the store's example of an escape, has exactly the curvature of the flat dust Friedmann universe with the same $\Lambda$ at the instant its expansion stops decelerating. So a density depending on curvature alone cannot single it out if the Friedmann universes are admissible. The stored counter-model survives only because its admissible class omits them. Conversely, the narrowing to fields whose arguments are constant is false without continuity: a degree-zero ratio of curvature scalars is constant along flat dust Friedmann although the scalars vary.

Matter is different. The square $Q$ of the departure from Einstein's equations at the calibrated coupling is a polynomial in curvature and stress. It vanishes on every solution at $G = 1$, so the density $\tfrac14(1 + cQ)$ leaves every standard solution admissible with density $\tfrac14$. Yet on an Einstein static universe the same density takes the value $\tfrac12$, with the Clausius relation satisfied and Newton's constant halved. What (Loc) adds on the integrated reading is curvature independence off the calibrated paths and one coupling for fields that never approach calibrated data.
synthesis.integrated-loc-curvature-claus.lay: To get Einstein's equations from heat flow across horizons, one assumes that every small piece of horizon carries the same entropy per unit area. Earlier work showed that the heat-flow law already forces this entropy to be the same throughout any one universe, but possibly different in different universes. This result asks when that loophole can actually be used. If the entropy depends smoothly on how strongly space is curved, the loophole closes for any universe that thins out toward empty space, and expanding universes of ordinary matter pass through every isotropic curvature on their way, including that of Einstein's static universe, the old example of an escape. If the entropy may also depend on the matter itself, the loophole stays open: an explicit rule gives the standard value in every ordinary universe and a different value, with a weaker gravity, in Einstein's static universe.
flags: beyond one flat chart: the Einstein static universe of (iii) and (v) has closed spatial sections; the statements are local and are made on its stereographic chart, an open part of flat spacetime

proofs.main:
Conventions as in the statement: the store sign of Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-gtg-dictionary}, $\hbar = c = G = 1$, $t = 2\pi T$. The check computes every curvature below from the gauge field itself, as exact Taylor jets of $\hb^{-1}$ about a rational point, the torsion-free $\Omega$ solved from them and the field strength read off.

\emph{The Clausius defect in this sign.} By Theorem \claimref{synthesis.einstein-equations-from-c-loc-and-clausius}(2), on a thin pencil about the generator through $p$ the defect $\delta Q - T_{\chi}\,\eta\,\delta A$ is $\tfrac{\kappa}{2}\bigl(T(k,k) - \tfrac{\eta}{2\pi}\Ric^{\circ}(k,k)\bigr)\lambda_{0}^{2}$ at leading order, with $\Ric^{\circ} = -\Ric$, the store's Ricci map being $\mathcal{R}(b)$. Hence the defect is $\tfrac{\kappa}{4\pi}\bigl(t(k,k) + \eta\,k\cdot\mathcal{R}(k)\bigr)\lambda_{0}^{2}$, and for a density constant on a connected field (H1) holds on every patch exactly when $t(k,k) + \eta\,k\cdot\mathcal{R}(k) = 0$ for every null $k$, that is (polarising over null directions) when the field equations hold with $G_{e} = 1/(4\eta)$ and some $\Lambda$, as in that theorem.

\emph{(i).} Let $U$ be an admissible field and $p_{n} \in U$ with local data converging to calibrated data $d_{*}$. Since $\eta = f(\text{local data})$ is $C^{1}$ on $U$ and (H1) holds on every patch, Theorem \claimref{synthesis.c-loc-entropy-clause-curvature-independent-density}(iv) gives $k\cdot D\eta = 0$ for every null $k$, hence $\eta$ is constant on the connected $U$. Continuity of $f$ gives $\eta = \lim f(\text{data}(p_{n})) = f(d_{*})$. For de Sitter data $f(d_{*}) = \tfrac14$: the de Sitter field's local data are the same at every point of a cut of its cosmological horizon, so the integrated density over a cut of area $4\pi N^{2}$ is $f(d_{*})\cdot 4\pi N^{2}$, and the stored de Sitter entropy $\pi N^{2}$ under the identification of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.c-loc-entropy-clause-curvature-independent-density}(ii) gives $f(d_{*}) = \tfrac14$. For flat data $f(0) = \lim_{\Lambda\to 0} f(\tfrac{\Lambda}{3}B, 0) = \tfrac14$ by continuity. So $\eta = \tfrac14$ on $U$, and by the defect identity the field equations hold with $G_{e} = 1/(4\eta) = 1$.

\emph{(ii).} For $\hb^{-1}(e_{i}) = a(t)\,e_{i}$ the coframe depends on $t$ alone and the curvature at a point depends on $(a, \dot a, \ddot a)$ there; with $a = 1$ the check computes, at four tabulated $(a_{1}, a_{2})$ and the de Sitter value, $\mathcal{R}(\gamma_{i}\wedge\gamma_{j}) = a_{1}^{2}\gamma_{i}\wedge\gamma_{j}$, $\mathcal{R}(\gamma_{0}\wedge\gamma_{i}) = a_{2}\gamma_{0}\wedge\gamma_{i}$, Weyl part zero. For a general instant this is the standard curvature of the flat Friedmann metric (cited from memory): the curvature is $(\dot a/a)^{2}$ on the space planes and $\ddot a/a$ on the time planes, linear in $(a_{1}^{2}, a_{2})$ at $a = 1$; the tabulated samples are a check of it in the store's sign, not a proof of the general formula. The Ricci map is then $\mathcal{R}(\gamma_{0}) = 3a_{2}\gamma_{0}$, $\mathcal{R}(\gamma_{i}) = (a_{2} + 2a_{1}^{2})\gamma_{i}$, and the field equations with a fluid at rest reduce to the two relations $a_{1}^{2} = (s + \Lambda)/3$ and $a_{2} = -s(1 + 3w)/6 + \Lambda/3$; the check verifies the field equations at five samples and that shifting $a_{2}$ breaks them. Substituting, $\mathcal{R} = \tfrac{\Lambda}{3}B + s\,K_{w}$ with $K_{w}$ equal to $\tfrac13$ on space planes and $-\tfrac{1+3w}{6}$ on time planes, so $\mathcal{R}$ is affine in $s$ and equals the de Sitter (or, at $\Lambda = 0$, flat) operator at $s = 0$.

Late times. The field equations' Bianchi identity gives $\dot\rho = -3\tfrac{\dot a}{a}(1+w)\rho$, so $\rho \propto a^{-3(1+w)}$. On the expanding branch $\dot a/a = ((s + \Lambda)/3)^{1/2} > 0$ never vanishes. If $\Lambda > 0$, $\dot a/a \ge (\Lambda/3)^{1/2}$ and $a \to \infty$ exponentially; if $\Lambda = 0$, $\dot a \propto a^{1 - 3(1+w)/2}$ gives $a \propto t^{2/(3(1+w))} \to \infty$. Either way $\rho$ decreases continuously to $0$ and $T \to 0$, so the local data tend to $(\tfrac{\Lambda}{3}B, 0)$, calibrated data.

Reach. Given $\beta > 0$ and $-2\beta \le \alpha < \beta$, put $w = 0$, $\Lambda = 2\alpha + \beta$ if $\alpha \ge -\beta/2$, and $w = -(2\alpha + \beta)/(3\beta)$, $\Lambda = 0$ otherwise; in both cases $w \in [0,1]$, $\Lambda \in [0, 3\beta)$, $s = 3\beta - \Lambda > 0$, and the two relations return $(a_{1}^{2}, a_{2}) = (\beta, \alpha)$ (tabulated grid in the check, with the controls $\alpha = \beta$, $\alpha < -2\beta$, $\beta \le 0$ outside the reach).

\emph{(iii).} If $f$ depends on the curvature only, each flat Friedmann field of (ii) is admissible by hypothesis and its local data tend to calibrated data, so by (i) $\eta = \tfrac14$ on it, at every instant; by the reach, $f = \tfrac14$ at every isotropic Weyl-free curvature with $\beta > 0$, $-2\beta \le \alpha < \beta$, and at $\alpha = \beta$ by the calibration itself. For the Einstein static universe the check computes the curvature from the stereographic gauge field $\hb^{-1}(e_{i}) = \tfrac{2A}{1 + |x|^{2}}e_{i}$ about $x = 0$ (a point of an open chart; the field is homogeneous, so the value holds at every point): it is Weyl-free with $\beta = 1/A^{2}$, $\alpha = 0$, equal to the flat Friedmann instant $a_{1} = 1/A$, $a_{2} = 0$, which by (ii) is the dust field with $\Lambda = 1/A^{2}$, $s = 2/A^{2}$ at its inflection instant; both satisfy the dust field equations with these values (checked at $A = 2, 3, \tfrac12$, with a mismatched radius as control). The density $\tfrac14(1 + c\,S_{ab}S^{ab})$ is a continuous function of the curvature, so it equals $\tfrac14$ there whenever the flat dust Friedmann-$\Lambda$ fields are admissible; in Theorem \claimref{synthesis.loc-independent-of-clausius-and-killing-data} its admissible class is defined by (H1) with that density, which requires $S_{ab}S^{ab}$ constant on each field, and $S_{ab}S^{ab} = \tfrac34 s^{2}$ varies along every flat dust Friedmann field, so those fields are not in it.

\emph{(iv).} Along flat dust Friedmann with $\Lambda = 0$ ($a_{1}^{2} = s/3$, $a_{2} = -s/6$) the check computes the scalar curvature and $S_{ab}S^{ab} = \mathcal{R}_{ab}\mathcal{R}^{ab} - \tfrac14\mathcal{R}^{2}$ from the gauge field at three instants: the scalar curvature takes three values and $S_{ab}S^{ab} = \tfrac34\mathcal{R}^{2}$ at each. So $\eta = \tfrac14(1 + c\,S_{ab}S^{ab}/\mathcal{R}^{2}) = \tfrac14(1 + \tfrac34 c)$ is constant on the field, and with $G_{e} = 1/(4\eta)$ the field equations hold for dust of density $\rho_{e} = \rho/G_{e}$ (the curvature fixes only $8\pi G_{e}\rho_{e}$), so the defect identity gives (H1) on every patch. At Ricci-flat data the quotient is undefined; no continuous extension takes the value $\tfrac14$ at flat data and $\tfrac14(1 + \tfrac34 c)$ along a path of data tending to flat data, by (i).

\emph{(v).} The trace-free part of $\mathcal{G}(b) + \Lambda b = -4t(b)$ is $\mathcal{R}^{\circ}(b) = -4t^{\circ}(b)$, since $\mathcal{G}$ and $\mathcal{R}$ differ by a multiple of the identity; so $X = 0$, $Q = 0$ and $\eta = \tfrac14$ on every pair satisfying the field equations at $G_{e} = 1$, and by the defect identity (H1) holds on all its patches (checked on three Friedmann samples). On the Einstein static universe of radius $2$ ($\mathcal{R}(\gamma_{0}) = 0$, $\mathcal{R}(\gamma_{i}) = \tfrac12\gamma_{i}$, scalar $\tfrac32$), with $t(b) = \sigma(b\cdot\gamma_{0})\gamma_{0}$: $\mathcal{R}^{\circ}(\gamma_{0}) = -\tfrac38\gamma_{0}$, $\mathcal{R}^{\circ}(\gamma_{i}) = \tfrac18\gamma_{i}$, $t^{\circ}(\gamma_{0}) = \tfrac34\sigma\gamma_{0}$, $t^{\circ}(\gamma_{i}) = -\tfrac14\sigma\gamma_{i}$, so $X = (\tfrac18 - \sigma)\,\mathrm{diag}(-3, 1, 1, 1)$ and $Q = 12(\tfrac18 - \sigma)^{2}$. The field equations with $G_{e} = 1/(4\eta)$, $\mathcal{G}(b) + \Lambda b = -t(b)/\eta$, give $\Lambda = \tfrac14$ and $\sigma = \eta/2$. At $\eta = \tfrac12$, $\sigma = \tfrac14$, $Q = \tfrac{3}{16}$ and $\tfrac14(1 + \tfrac{16}{3}\cdot\tfrac{3}{16}) = \tfrac12$: the density of the model takes the value $\eta$ that the field's own Clausius balance needs. The check computes $Q$, the field equations and the defect $t(k,k) + \eta\,k\cdot\mathcal{R}(k) = 0$ at five null $k$ from the gauge field, together with the second fixed point $\eta = \tfrac14$, $\sigma = \tfrac18$, $Q = 0$ (the same universe at $G_{e} = 1$), and a control (the density $\tfrac14$ with $\sigma = \tfrac14$ leaves a nonzero defect). The field is homogeneous and its symmetries fix the dust's rest frame, so $Q$ and $\eta$ are constant on it, $\eta$ is $C^{1}$, and (H1) holds on every patch on the integrated reading. $\eta$ is a polynomial in the local data, continuous everywhere, and $\tfrac14$ at calibrated data ($X = 0$ there).

\emph{(vi).} By (i) and (iii), under continuity the Clausius relation and calibration force $\eta = \tfrac14$ wherever the admissible class carries the local data to calibrated data, and by (iii) the flat Friedmann fields do so for every isotropic Weyl-free curvature in the stated range; (Loc)'s curvature clause adds content only at curvature values outside every such path. By (v), a density depending on matter is not constrained off the locus of Einstein's equations at the calibrated coupling, on any field none of whose points has data near calibrated data; (Loc)'s matter clause, read through Theorem \claimref{synthesis.einstein-equations-from-c-loc-and-clausius}, is the statement that such fields have the coupling $G_{e} = 1$ too. Neither part uses a property of the series beyond the stored theorems cited; the result is transport-absent.

synthesis.inverse-frame-free-tractor-gau.technical:
The open problem asks why the gravitational action should be varied over $\Cl(2,4)$ connections that preserve the frozen point $I$, given that on the series' own transport, the normal tractor connection, preserving $I$ is the Einstein condition. This result restates that field space by hypotheses that mention neither $I$ nor any field equation; it is a premise exchange, an equivalent reading of the premise that the varied connection admits a parallel tractor $I$ with $\ip{X}{I} = 1$, not a derivation from transport. Build a $\Cl(2,4)$ gauge field from the two gauge fields of gauge theory gravity and nothing else, the position-gauge field $\hb$ (through its soldering form $e = \hb^{-1}$) and the rotation-gauge field $\Omega$; require it to transform as a gauge field under the rotations and displacements of gauge theory gravity; solder the canonical tractor to the frame; and either forbid the inverse frame $\hb$ or forbid derivatives. Either restriction makes every slot linear in $e$ and $\Omega$ (by displacement weight, or by moving any frame to any other with a linear displacement), and Lorentz covariance then leaves exactly $A_{ho} = \Omega - 
Inf \wedge e + ho\,
O \wedge e$ with $ho$ constant. This field annihilates the constant tractor $
Inf + ho\,
O$ for every gravitational field, and nothing else, with $\Lambda = 6ho$ left to the registered input. Conversely every connection with a parallel tractor of unit pairing with $X$ takes this form in a suitable gauge, so the two statements of the premise are equivalent.

The series' transport has the Schouten map in the last slot, which needs both derivatives and the inverse frame: it scales as $1/c$ when the frame is scaled by $c$ and has a pole where the frame drops rank. It coincides with $A_{ho}$ exactly on Einstein fields, so the restriction that would assume the answer is never made. The limits are stated: without the two-field premise an independent special-conformal field is also polynomial and preserves no tractor, and a frozen point treated as a Higgs field reduces the connection only when infinitely stiff; and the covariance asked for is that of gauge theory gravity, not the larger parabolic group with which the store gauges the tractor field, under which the reduction is only a choice of gauge for a connection that admits a parallel tractor. Transport supplies neither restriction; the one series reading of the first is that the gauge field be defined on the corank-one walls where the frame degenerates, which the series asks for there but not at the Kasner wall.
synthesis.inverse-frame-free-tractor-gau.lay: Earlier work found that the series' formula for gravity gives Einstein's equations only if one assumes in advance which shapes of the gravitational field are allowed: those that keep a special fixed direction, the frozen point, unchanged. This result asks what could justify that assumption without assuming Einstein's equations. It builds the six-dimensional field from the two ingredients of gauge theory gravity and nothing else, and adds one rule: never divide by the frame that measures lengths, or alternatively never use rates of change. Either rule forces the field into a single form, and every field of that form keeps one fixed direction unchanged, which is the frozen point. So these rules are another way of stating the assumption, not a reason for it. The series' own way of carrying directions from point to point breaks both rules, and agrees with the forced form only where Einstein's equations already hold. The rules are not derived from the series, and they work only together with the premise that there are just two ingredients.
